lessons.title: 1.1 Welcome to the Course
lessons.html:
📖 Welcome to the Course
A clear path from where you are now to the score your college asks for.

Key Words & Meanings

Tap a word to open its definition.

Digital SAT

The computer-delivered SAT used to measure college-readiness skills.

baseline score

A starting score used to identify present strengths and gaps.

score goal

A specific result a learner aims to achieve.

diagnostic test

An assessment used to identify areas requiring study.

This course prepares you for the Digital SAT, the version College Board has used worldwide since 2023. Everything here matches that test: two sections, adaptive modules, the Bluebook app, and a 400–1600 total.

Work in order. Modules 1–6 build Reading & Writing, 7–11 build Math, 12 covers digital test strategy, and 13 is where you sit full mock exams. Each lesson is a video, a note like this one, and a short quiz you must pass to unlock the next lesson.

Key points

  • The Digital SAT is 2 hours 14 minutes of testing, not the old 3 hours.
  • There is no penalty for a wrong answer, so you answer every question.
  • Colleges see your total (400–1600) and your two section scores (200–800 each).
  • Consistency beats intensity: one lesson a day for eight weeks beats one long weekend.
  • Keep an error log from lesson 1. It becomes the most valuable file you own.
  • You need the Final Assessment in Module 13 to earn your certificate.

Example

Fatu in Monrovia wants a 1200. She takes a diagnostic in week one, scores 980, and sees that Math costs her more than Reading. She spends four evenings a week on Math and two on Reading & Writing, and re-tests every fortnight rather than guessing whether she has improved.

Why this matters

Most candidates who miss their target did not lack ability. They studied whatever felt comfortable instead of whatever was costing them points, and they found out too late.

lessons.title: 1.2 What is the SAT?
lessons.html:
📖 What is the SAT?
One standardised test that lets colleges compare applicants from anywhere.

Key Words & Meanings

Tap a word to open its definition.

SAT

A standardized college-admission assessment administered by College Board.

standardized test

An assessment given and scored under consistent conditions.

college readiness

The knowledge and skills needed for entry-level college work.

admission

The process through which an institution accepts applicants.

The SAT is a college admission test run by the College Board. It measures reading, writing and mathematical reasoning — not what any one school happened to teach you — so an applicant from Liberia and one from Ohio can be compared on the same scale.

Most United States colleges accept it, and many scholarship programmes use it as a cut-off. Some colleges are now test-optional, but a strong score still helps, and for international applicants seeking funding it often matters more, not less.

Key points

  • The SAT tests reasoning with reading, writing and maths, not memorised facts.
  • It is written and administered by the College Board.
  • Scores are used for admission, scholarships and sometimes course placement.
  • SAT scores are generally valid for five years.
  • Test-optional means a college will consider you without a score — not that a good score is ignored.
  • The SAT is not the ACT; they are separate tests and most colleges accept either.

Example

A student applying to five American universities finds three are test-optional and two require a score. She sits the SAT anyway: the two requiring it will not read her file without one, and one of the test-optional three awards merit scholarships using SAT bands.

Why this matters

Knowing what the test is for tells you how hard to push. A score that only unlocks admission is a different target from one that has to win you funding.

lessons.title: 1.3 SAT Test Format
lessons.html:
📖 SAT Test Format
Two sections, four modules, and a structure that never changes.

Key Words & Meanings

Tap a word to open its definition.

module

One timed part of a Digital SAT section.

section

A major tested area: Reading and Writing or Math.

multiple choice

A question answered by selecting from listed options.

student-produced response

A Math answer entered by the test taker rather than selected.

The Digital SAT has two sections: Reading & Writing and Math. Each section is split into two modules, and each module is separately timed. Reading & Writing gives you 27 questions in 32 minutes per module; Math gives you 22 questions in 35 minutes per module.

Reading & Writing questions are short: one passage of about 25–150 words with a single question attached. You never face a long passage with ten questions hanging off it, the way the paper test worked.

Key points

  • Reading & Writing – 2 modules, 27 questions each, 32 minutes each.
  • Math – 2 modules, 22 questions each, 35 minutes each.
  • There is a 10-minute break between the two sections.
  • Each Reading & Writing question has its own short passage.
  • About 75% of Math is multiple choice; the rest are student-produced responses you type in.
  • A built-in Desmos graphing calculator is available for the whole Math section.

Example

In Reading & Writing you might see a 60-word paragraph about cassava farming followed by one question on the author's main point — then a completely unrelated 40-word paragraph for the next question. Short, self-contained, and fast.

Why this matters

Knowing the format removes surprise on test day, and surprise is expensive: a candidate expecting long passages wastes the first minutes of module one adjusting instead of answering.

lessons.title: 1.4 SAT Scoring System (400–1600)
lessons.html:
📖 SAT Scoring System (400–1600)
Two section scores, added together, and nothing subtracted for a wrong answer.

Key Words & Meanings

Tap a word to open its definition.

scaled score

A score converted from performance using an established scoring process.

section score

The 200–800 result for one SAT section.

total score

The sum of the two section scores.

score range

The lowest through highest possible score values.

Reading & Writing is scored 200–800 and Math is scored 200–800. Your total is simply the two added, so the scale runs 400–1600. There is no separate essay score; the essay was retired.

Raw correct answers are converted to scaled scores through a process called equating, which adjusts for small differences in difficulty between test forms. This is why you cannot compute your score by counting correct answers, and why a slightly harder form does not disadvantage you.

Key points

  • Total = Reading & Writing (200–800) + Math (200–800), so 400–1600.
  • No penalty for wrong answers — always answer, always guess if you must.
  • Roughly 1050 is around the national average; 1200+ is competitive; 1400+ is selective.
  • Equating means the same performance earns the same score on any test form.
  • Because the test is adaptive, harder second modules make the top of the range reachable.
  • You can send scores to colleges and, with Score Choice, choose which sitting to send.

Example

Moses scores 610 Reading & Writing and 590 Math. His total is 1200, which clears the 1150 cut-off for his university's international scholarship. Had he left six questions blank rather than guessing, that total would very likely have started with an 11.

Why this matters

Understanding the scale sets a realistic target and shows which section to work on. Adding 60 points to a weak Math score is usually far easier than squeezing the last 20 out of a strong Reading score.

lessons.title: 1.5 Digital SAT Overview
lessons.html:
📖 Digital SAT Overview
The test adapts to you, and that changes how the first module matters.

Key Words & Meanings

Tap a word to open its definition.

adaptive testing

A format in which later question difficulty depends partly on earlier performance.

Bluebook

College Board's application for taking the Digital SAT.

Desmos

The built-in graphing calculator available during Math.

annotation

A digital mark or note used to identify important information.

The Digital SAT is multistage adaptive. You sit module 1 of a section; the app scores it instantly and routes you into either an easier or a harder module 2. Both routes are scored fairly, but only the harder route reaches the top of the 200–800 range.

This is not adaptive question by question — within a module you can move freely, flag questions and come back. The adaptation happens once, between the two modules.

Key points

  • Adaptation happens between modules, not between questions.
  • Module 1 performance decides whether module 2 is the easier or harder form.
  • Within a module you may skip, flag and return as much as you like.
  • The harder module 2 unlocks the upper part of the section's score range.
  • Both sections adapt independently: a strong Math module 1 does not affect Reading.
  • Never rush module 1 to save time for module 2 — module 1 sets your ceiling.

Example

Two students each answer 30 of 54 Reading & Writing questions correctly. The one who got more of them right in module 1 was routed to the harder module 2 and scores higher, because that route is scaled to a higher band. Same total correct, different score.

Why this matters

Most SAT advice written before 2023 assumes a fixed test where every question counts the same. On the Digital SAT, treating module 1 as the more important half is a genuine strategy change.

lessons.title: 1.6 Study Plan
lessons.html:
📖 Study Plan
A plan turns a 1600-point scale into this evening's task.

Key Words & Meanings

Tap a word to open its definition.

study plan

A scheduled program of learning activities connected to a goal.

spaced practice

Study distributed across multiple sessions rather than crowded into one.

accuracy rate

The percentage of attempted questions answered correctly.

error log

A record of mistakes, causes, corrections, and review dates.

Start with a diagnostic full test so you know your real starting score and, more importantly, which section is costing you more. Then set a target and a test date and work backwards.

A workable eight-week shape: weeks 1–2 fundamentals in your weaker section, weeks 3–5 topic drills across both, weeks 6–7 timed modules, week 8 full mocks and taper. Adjust the weeks, keep the order.

Key points

  • Diagnose first. Studying before you know your weak section wastes the first fortnight.
  • Give the weaker section roughly twice the time of the stronger one.
  • Study in focused blocks of 45 minutes rather than open-ended sessions.
  • Take a full timed mock every two weeks, not every day.
  • Log every wrong answer with why it was wrong, not just the correct letter.
  • Do the final full mock about five days before the test, then taper.

Example

Fatu scores 980 on her diagnostic: 540 Reading & Writing, 440 Math. She gives Math four evenings a week and Reading two, keeps Sunday for reviewing her error log, and re-tests on alternate Saturdays. By week six her Math is 520 and her plan shifts to timed modules.

Why this matters

Without a plan, students practise what feels comfortable. The error log and the fortnightly mock are what stop that, because both make avoidance visible.

lessons.title: 1.7 Registration Process
lessons.html:
📖 Registration Process
Register early, because seats at a centre run out before the deadline does.

Key Words & Meanings

Tap a word to open its definition.

registration

The formal process of booking a test administration.

deadline

The final date by which an action must be completed.

test center

An approved location where the SAT is administered.

confirmation

Official evidence that registration has been completed.

You register through your College Board account at collegeboard.org: create the account, choose a test date, choose a test centre, upload a photo and pay the fee. International test centres are fewer and fill quickly, so book as soon as dates open.

The photo you upload has to match the identity document you will bring. Your name on the registration must match that document exactly — a middle name on one and not the other is enough to cause trouble at the door.

Key points

  • Register through your own College Board account, not a third party.
  • International seats are limited; book as early as dates are released.
  • Your registration name must match your passport exactly.
  • The uploaded photo must be a clear, recent head-and-shoulders image of you.
  • Note the regular deadline and the late-registration deadline — late costs extra.
  • Print or save the admission ticket; you need it with your ID on the day.

Example

A student registers as Musu Kollie but her passport reads Musu B. Kollie. She corrects the registration a week before the date. Had she left it, the centre could have refused her entry with no refund.

Why this matters

Registration is the cheapest part of the process to get right and among the most expensive to get wrong: a rejected entry means paying again and waiting months for the next international date.

lessons.title: 1.8 Test-Day Rules
lessons.html:
📖 Test-Day Rules
The rules are simple, and breaking one can void a score you already earned.

Key Words & Meanings

Tap a word to open its definition.

valid identification

An accepted document confirming a test taker's identity.

prohibited device

Technology not permitted for use during testing.

test security

Rules protecting the fairness and integrity of the assessment.

dismissal

Removal from the test because of a serious rule violation.

Bring an acceptable photo ID and your admission ticket. Bring your own fully charged laptop or tablet with Bluebook installed, or use a centre device if you requested one. Bring a charger, and an approved calculator if you prefer your own to the built-in Desmos.

Phones, smart watches and any recording device must be off and away for the whole session, including the break. Being seen with one is grounds for cancelling your score, not just a warning.

Key points

  • Acceptable ID: a valid passport for international candidates.
  • Your device must be charged and have Bluebook installed and updated beforehand.
  • Complete exam setup in Bluebook in the days before, not on the morning.
  • Phones and smart watches off and stored — through the break as well.
  • Arrive early; doors close and latecomers are not admitted.
  • You may not discuss or share test content afterwards; doing so can void your score.

Example

A candidate finishes module 1, checks the time on a smart watch during the break, and is reported. The score for a test he had already half-completed is cancelled. Nothing about his English or his maths was in question.

Why this matters

Every rule here is about protecting the score you spent months building. They cost nothing to follow and everything to ignore.

lessons.title: 1.9 Using the Bluebook Testing App
lessons.html:
📖 Using the Bluebook Testing App
The app is not just a screen; its tools are worth points.

Key Words & Meanings

Tap a word to open its definition.

exam setup

The required Bluebook process that prepares a registered test.

device check

Verification that a computer meets testing requirements.

reference sheet

A built-in list of approved Math formulas.

proctor

The person responsible for supervising a test session.

Bluebook is College Board's testing application, and everything happens inside it: the timer, the questions, the annotation tool, the flag tool, the reference sheet and the Desmos graphing calculator. Install it and run exam setup well before test day.

Learn the tools in practice, not on the day. Every minute spent working out how to graph an equation in Desmos during the test is a minute not spent answering.

Key points

  • Flag a hard question, move on, and return before the module ends.
  • Annotate lets you highlight passage text and attach a note.
  • Option eliminator crosses out answers you have ruled out.
  • The Desmos graphing calculator is available for the entire Math section.
  • A reference sheet of geometry formulas is built in — you need not memorise those.
  • Bluebook has full-length practice tests; use them so the interface feels ordinary.

Example

On a hard quadratic, instead of factoring under pressure, a student types the equation into Desmos and reads the x-intercepts off the graph in about fifteen seconds. Same answer, a fraction of the risk.

Why this matters

The students who gain most from the digital format are the ones who practised inside Bluebook. The tools are free, they are the same on test day, and they turn some hard questions into fast ones.

lessons.title: 2.1 Academic Vocabulary
lessons.html:
📖 Academic Vocabulary
The SAT tests words you meet in real texts, not a memorised rare-word list.

Key Words & Meanings

Tap a word to open its definition.

academic vocabulary

Formal words commonly used in educational and scholarly texts.

precision

The quality of expressing an idea exactly.

connotation

A feeling or association carried by a word.

context

The surrounding information that helps determine meaning.

The Digital SAT dropped obscure vocabulary. What it tests now is high-utility academic words — the ones that appear across history, science and social science writing: undermine, plausible, arbitrary, nuanced, comprehensive, novel, sustain, warrant.

These words are tested in context. You are shown a short passage with a blank or an underlined word and asked which choice best fits the meaning as the author uses it, which is often not the word's most common meaning.

Key points

  • Learn academic words, not rare ones — the test moved away from obscurity.
  • Many tested words have a common meaning and a scholarly one; the scholarly one is usually correct.
  • Learn each word with a sentence, never as a bare definition.
  • Watch for words with positive or negative charge: undermine is negative, bolster positive.
  • Ten words learned properly beat a hundred skimmed.
  • Reading serious journalism daily builds this faster than any list.

Example

Novel usually means a book. In “The team proposed a novel approach to flood control” it means new. The SAT would offer fictional as a trap, because it matches the common meaning rather than the sentence.

Why this matters

Vocabulary in context appears in every Reading & Writing module. Because the words are academic rather than rare, this is one of the most improvable areas on the whole test.

lessons.title: 2.2 Grammar Basics
lessons.html:
📖 Grammar Basics
A small set of rules produces most of the Standard English Conventions questions.

Key Words & Meanings

Tap a word to open its definition.

grammar

The system of rules governing how words form meaningful sentences.

subject

The person, thing, or idea a clause is about.

predicate

The part of a clause stating what the subject does or is.

agreement

The grammatical matching of related sentence elements.

Roughly a quarter of Reading & Writing is grammar, and it is tested from a short list: subject–verb agreement, pronouns, verb tense, modifiers, parallel structure, punctuation between clauses, and transitions.

SAT grammar has right and wrong answers, not stylistic preferences. That makes it the most reliably improvable part of the test: learn the rule, apply it, get the point.

Key points

  • A clause has a subject and a verb; an independent clause can stand alone.
  • Two independent clauses may not be joined by a comma alone (a comma splice).
  • A verb agrees with its subject, not with whatever noun sits nearest it.
  • A pronoun must agree with its antecedent and refer to it unambiguously.
  • Keep tense consistent unless the meaning genuinely requires a change.
  • When two answers mean the same thing, the shorter one is usually right.

Example

“The list of required documents were posted.” The subject is list, singular, not documents. Correct: “The list of required documents was posted.” The prepositional phrase between them is there to mislead you.

Why this matters

Grammar questions are quick and rule-based, so they are the cheapest points on the test. A student who masters this list can pick up 40–60 scaled points in a fortnight.

lessons.title: 2.3 Sentence Structure
lessons.html:
📖 Sentence Structure
Almost every punctuation question is really a question about clause boundaries.

Key Words & Meanings

Tap a word to open its definition.

independent clause

A word group with a subject and verb that expresses a complete thought.

dependent clause

A word group with a subject and verb that cannot stand alone.

compound sentence

Two independent clauses joined correctly.

complex sentence

An independent clause combined with at least one dependent clause.

A simple sentence is one independent clause. A compound sentence joins two independent clauses. A complex sentence joins an independent clause to a dependent one. Recognising which you have tells you what punctuation is legal.

The practical method: cover the punctuation and ask whether each side could stand alone as a sentence. Two standalone sides need a full stop, a semicolon, or a comma plus and, but, or, nor, for, so, yet. One standalone side and one fragment usually take a comma or nothing.

Key points

  • Test each side of the punctuation: could it stand alone?
  • Independent + independent → period, semicolon, or comma + FANBOYS.
  • Dependent + independent → comma after the dependent part.
  • Independent + dependent → usually no comma.
  • A colon must follow a complete sentence, and introduces an explanation or list.
  • A dash can work like a comma or a colon, but must be used consistently in a pair.

Example

“The rains arrived late ___ the harvest was poor.” Both sides stand alone, so a comma alone is wrong. Legal: a semicolon, a period, or “late, so the harvest was poor”.

Why this matters

Once you test clause boundaries mechanically, punctuation questions stop being about instinct. This single habit is worth several points in every Reading & Writing module.

questions.explanation: On the SAT a colon must be preceded by an independent clause, and it introduces an explanation or list.

lessons.title: 2.4 Parts of Speech
lessons.html:
📖 Parts of Speech
Naming the job a word does is how you spot the error.

Key Words & Meanings

Tap a word to open its definition.

part of speech

A category based on the function a word performs.

noun

A word naming a person, place, thing, or idea.

verb

A word expressing action, occurrence, or state.

modifier

A word or phrase that describes or limits another element.

Nouns name; verbs act; adjectives describe nouns; adverbs describe verbs, adjectives or other adverbs; pronouns replace nouns; prepositions place things in time or space; conjunctions join.

You are not tested on the labels. You are tested on consequences of them — whether a describing word should be quick or quickly, whether a pronoun should be who or whom, whether a phrase is describing the right noun.

Key points

  • Adjectives modify nouns; adverbs modify verbs, adjectives and other adverbs.
  • Good is an adjective, well is the adverb: she writes well.
  • Who is a subject pronoun, whom an object pronoun.
  • Fewer is for countable nouns, less for uncountable amounts.
  • A preposition is always followed by a noun or noun phrase, never by a clause subject.
  • Identify the subject by asking who or what performs the verb.

Example

“The engine runs ___.” The word describes runs, a verb, so it must be an adverb: smoothly, not smooth. The same logic decides fewer farmers (countable) against less rainfall (uncountable).

Why this matters

Every grammar rule the SAT tests refers to a part of speech. Being able to name what a word is doing turns a guess into a decision.

lessons.html: Quick check: Review the lesson notes and work the two practice questions, then answer these to confirm you understood Parts of Speech.

questions.question: In 'The engine runs ___', which form is correct?
questions.explanation: The word describes the verb 'runs', so an adverb is required.

questions.question: Which is correct: 'fewer' or 'less'?
questions.explanation: 'Fewer' is used with countable nouns such as farmers; 'less' is used with uncountable amounts such as rainfall.

questions.question: What does an adverb modify?
questions.explanation: Adverbs modify verbs, adjectives and other adverbs, while adjectives modify nouns.

lessons.title: 2.5 Punctuation Rules
lessons.html:
📖 Punctuation Rules
Four marks, one decision each, and no room for taste.

Key Words & Meanings

Tap a word to open its definition.

punctuation

Marks used to organize writing and clarify meaning.

comma splice

The incorrect joining of independent clauses with only a comma.

semicolon

A mark joining closely related independent clauses.

colon

A mark introducing an explanation, example, or list after a complete clause.

The SAT tests commas, semicolons, colons and dashes, plus apostrophes. Each has a narrow legal use, and the test never asks which is prettier — only which is correct given the clause structure around it.

The most common trap is punctuation that separates a subject from its verb, or that cuts a sentence where nothing needs cutting. When no rule requires a mark, the answer with no mark is usually right.

Key points

  • Comma: after an introductory element, around non-essential information, in lists.
  • Semicolon: joins two independent clauses; also separates list items containing commas.
  • Colon: after a complete sentence, introducing an explanation or list.
  • Dashes: interrupt a sentence — use them in a matched pair.
  • Never separate a subject from its verb with a single comma.
  • Its is possessive; it's means it is or it has.

Example

“The report, which the committee published in March, recommends three changes.” The clause is non-essential, so it takes a matched pair of commas. Remove one and the sentence is wrong; remove both and it is also acceptable but changes emphasis.

Why this matters

Punctuation is roughly a fifth of the grammar questions and is entirely rule-driven. Learning four rules properly is faster than any amount of reading practice.

lessons.title: 📝 Practice: Punctuation Rules
lessons.html: Quick check: Review the lesson notes and work the two practice questions, then answer these to confirm you understood Punctuation Rules.

questions.question: Which mark correctly joins two independent clauses without a conjunction?
questions.explanation: A semicolon joins two independent clauses; a comma alone would create a comma splice.

questions.question: Non-essential information inside a sentence should be:
options: Enclosed in a matched pair of commas or dashes
Preceded by a single comma only
questions.explanation: Non-essential elements need matching punctuation on both sides, either two commas or two dashes.

questions.question: Which sentence uses 'its' correctly?
questions.explanation: 'Its' is the possessive form; 'it's' is a contraction of 'it is' or 'it has'.

lessons.title: 2.6 Transition Words
lessons.html:
📖 Transition Words
The right transition is decided by logic, not by how the sentence sounds.

Key Words & Meanings

Tap a word to open its definition.

transition

A word or phrase showing the relationship between ideas.

logical relationship

A connection such as contrast, cause, or continuation.

concession

Acknowledgment of an opposing or limiting point.

sequence

The order in which events or ideas occur.

Transition questions give you a blank between two sentences and four connecting words. The method is mechanical: read both sentences, decide the relationship between them in your own words, then pick the transition that matches.

There are only a few relationships to recognise — contrast, addition, cause, example, sequence, concession, emphasis. Learn which words signal each and the questions become almost automatic.

Key points

  • Contrast: however, nevertheless, by contrast, on the other hand.
  • Addition: moreover, furthermore, in addition, similarly.
  • Cause and effect: therefore, consequently, thus, as a result.
  • Example: for example, for instance, specifically.
  • Concession: admittedly, granted, to be sure.
  • Name the relationship before you look at the four choices.

Example

“Yields rose in the north. ___, they fell sharply in the south.” The relationship is contrast, so However is right and Therefore, Moreover and For example are all wrong — regardless of which sounds smoothest.

Why this matters

Transitions appear several times in every Reading & Writing module and are pure logic, so they reward method rather than reading speed.

lessons.title: 📝 Practice: Transition Words
lessons.html: Quick check: Review the lesson notes and work the two practice questions, then answer these to confirm you understood Transition Words.

questions.question: 'Yields rose in the north. ___, they fell sharply in the south.' Which transition fits?
questions.explanation: The two sentences contrast, so a contrast transition such as 'However' is required.

questions.question: What should you do before looking at the four transition choices?
options: Name the relationship between the two sentences yourself
questions.explanation: Deciding the logical relationship first prevents you from choosing a transition that merely sounds smooth.

questions.question: Which word signals cause and effect?
questions.explanation: 'Consequently' signals that the second statement results from the first.

lessons.title: 2.7 Context Clues
lessons.html:
📖 Context Clues
The passage always tells you what the word means; the skill is noticing where.

Key Words & Meanings

Tap a word to open its definition.

context clue

Nearby information that helps reveal a word's meaning.

definition clue

A direct explanation placed near an unfamiliar word.

contrast clue

An opposite idea used to clarify meaning.

inference

A logical conclusion drawn from textual evidence.

When you meet an unfamiliar word, the surrounding sentence usually defines it in one of four ways: by definition, by contrast, by example, or by cause and effect. Recognising which clue is present tells you where to look.

The most reliable habit is to cover the answer choices, predict a simple word of your own that fits the blank, and only then compare it against the options. Predicting first stops the wrong-but-familiar choice from capturing you.

Key points

  • Definition clue: the meaning is restated after a comma or dash.
  • Contrast clue: but, although, unlike, whereas signal an opposite meaning nearby.
  • Example clue: such as, for instance illustrate the word.
  • Cause clue: because, therefore, so tie the word to a result.
  • Predict your own simple word before reading the options.
  • Check the charge: does the sentence want something positive or negative?

Example

“Unlike her ebullient brother, Sarah was reserved and quiet.” Unlike is a contrast clue, and the contrast is with reserved and quiet, so ebullient must mean lively or enthusiastic — without ever having seen the word before.

Why this matters

Context clues let you answer vocabulary questions containing words you do not know, which is exactly the situation the test is designed to create.

lessons.title: 📝 Practice: Context Clues
lessons.html: Quick check: Review the lesson notes and work the two practice questions, then answer these to confirm you understood Context Clues.

questions.question: In 'Unlike her ebullient brother, Sarah was reserved and quiet', 'ebullient' most nearly means:
questions.explanation: 'Unlike' signals contrast with 'reserved and quiet', so 'ebullient' must mean lively or enthusiastic.

questions.question: Which words signal a contrast context clue?
questions.explanation: Contrast clues are introduced by words like although, whereas and unlike, which point to an opposite meaning.

questions.question: What should you do before reading the answer choices on a vocabulary question?
options: Predict a simple word of your own that fits
questions.explanation: Predicting your own word first prevents a familiar but incorrect choice from steering you.

lessons.title: 2.8 Reading Strategies
lessons.html:
📖 Reading Strategies
On the Digital SAT, read the question first — the passages are short enough to allow it.

Key Words & Meanings

Tap a word to open its definition.

active reading

Purposeful reading focused on structure, claims, and evidence.

evidence

Textual information supporting a conclusion.

paraphrase

The same meaning expressed in different words.

elimination

Removing options that conflict with the text or task.

Digital SAT passages run about 25–150 words with a single question each, so the old advice about mapping long passages no longer applies. Read the question, then read the passage knowing what you are looking for.

Answer in your own words before looking at the options. Then find the choice that matches your answer, rather than judging four choices in isolation — three of them are written to sound reasonable.

Key points

  • Read the question first; each passage serves only one question.
  • Answer in your own words, then match to a choice.
  • The correct answer is always supported by the text — you must be able to point at it.
  • Eliminate choices that are true in the world but absent from the passage.
  • Watch extreme words: always, never, all, only are rarely correct.
  • Do not spend more than about 70 seconds on a Reading & Writing question.

Example

A passage describes a study finding a link between soil pH and yield. A choice reading “soil pH is the most important factor in crop yield” is a trap: the passage showed a link, not primacy. The word most is doing the damage.

Why this matters

Every Reading & Writing question is answerable from its own short passage. Making yourself point at the supporting words is what separates a reliable 650 from an inconsistent 550.

lessons.title: 📝 Practice: Reading Strategies
lessons.html: Quick check: Review the lesson notes and work the two practice questions, then answer these to confirm you understood Reading Strategies.

questions.question: How long is a typical Digital SAT Reading & Writing passage?
questions.explanation: Digital SAT passages are short, roughly 25 to 150 words, each paired with a single question.

questions.question: What is the recommended order of work on a Reading & Writing question?
options: Read the passage, then the choices, then the question
Read the question, then the passage, then predict an answer
questions.explanation: Reading the question first tells you what to look for in the short passage, and predicting guards against trap choices.

questions.question: Why are choices containing 'always' or 'never' often wrong?
questions.explanation: Academic passages usually make qualified claims, so absolute wording overstates what the text supports.

lessons.title: 2.9 Critical Thinking Skills
lessons.html:
📖 Critical Thinking Skills
The SAT rewards the reader who can tell a claim from the evidence for it.

Key Words & Meanings

Tap a word to open its definition.

critical thinking

Careful analysis and evaluation of information before reaching a conclusion.

claim

A statement presented as true or arguable.

assumption

An unstated idea accepted as part of an argument.

reasoning

The logical connection between evidence and a conclusion.

Most Reading & Writing questions are really asking one of three things: what is being claimed, what evidence supports it, and what would weaken or strengthen it. Learning to separate those three parts in any passage covers a large share of the section.

A claim is an assertion. Evidence is data, observation or citation offered for it. An assumption is what must be true for the evidence to support the claim — and unstated assumptions are where the test hides its hardest questions.

Key points

  • Separate claim, evidence and assumption as you read.
  • Correlation is not causation, and the SAT tests that distinction often.
  • To weaken an argument, attack its assumption or offer an alternative explanation.
  • To strengthen one, rule out an alternative explanation.
  • A conclusion cannot be broader than the evidence given for it.
  • Beware sample problems: a study of one village does not support a national claim.

Example

A passage reports that students who eat breakfast score higher, and concludes breakfast improves scores. The assumption is that nothing else differs between the groups. A choice noting that breakfast-eaters also sleep more weakens it by offering an alternative explanation.

Why this matters

Command-of-evidence and inference questions are the largest question group in Reading & Writing. They test reasoning about text, so they improve through method rather than through reading more.

lessons.title: 📝 Practice: Critical Thinking Skills
lessons.html: Quick check: Review the lesson notes and work the two practice questions, then answer these to confirm you understood Critical Thinking Skills.

questions.question: What is an assumption in an argument?
options: The first sentence of the passage
Something that must be true for the evidence to support the claim
questions.explanation: An assumption is the unstated link that the argument depends on, which is why attacking it weakens the argument.

questions.question: A study finds breakfast-eaters score higher and concludes breakfast raises scores. Which choice most weakens it?
options: Breakfast-eaters in the study also slept significantly more
questions.explanation: An alternative explanation for the same result undermines the causal conclusion drawn from a correlation.

questions.question: Which statement about conclusions is correct?
options: A conclusion may be broader than its evidence
A conclusion must not be broader than its evidence
Evidence and conclusion are the same thing
questions.explanation: Overreaching, drawing a conclusion wider than the evidence supports, is a common SAT trap answer.

lessons.title: 3.1 Finding Main Ideas
lessons.html:
📖 Finding Main Ideas
The main idea is what the whole passage is for, not the most striking sentence in it.

Key Words & Meanings

Tap a word to open its definition.

main idea

The central point that unifies all important details in a text.

scope

The range of information covered by an answer choice.

supporting detail

A fact or example that develops the main idea.

summary

A brief statement of the text's essential ideas.

A main-idea question asks for the central claim of a short passage. The trap answers are usually true statements taken from a single sentence — accurate, but too narrow to be what the passage is doing.

The reliable method is to summarise the passage in your own words in one short sentence before you look at the options, then reject any choice that is narrower than your summary, wider than it, or about something the passage only mentioned in passing.

Key points

  • The main idea covers the whole passage, not one sentence of it.
  • Too narrow is the most common trap: a true detail offered as the main point.
  • Too broad is the second: a claim the passage never supports in full.
  • The last sentence often states or restates the main idea.
  • Summarise in your own words before reading the options.
  • If a choice introduces a subject the passage never discusses, eliminate it immediately.

Example

A passage explains that a soil study found three factors affecting yield and that pH mattered most. “pH affects crop yield” is too narrow; “Agriculture depends on soil science” is too broad. The main idea is that of the three factors studied, pH proved the most influential.

Why this matters

Main-idea questions appear in every Reading & Writing module, and the same too-narrow / too-broad test also settles many summary and purpose questions.

lessons.title: 📝 Practice: Finding Main Ideas
lessons.html: Quick check: Review the lesson notes and work the two practice questions, then answer these to confirm you understood Finding Main Ideas.

questions.question: What is the most common trap answer on a main-idea question?
options: A statement that contradicts the passage
A true detail from one sentence, too narrow to be the main point
questions.explanation: Trap answers are often accurate details lifted from a single sentence, which are too narrow to be the central claim.

questions.question: What should you do before reading the answer choices?
options: Summarise the passage in one sentence of your own
questions.explanation: Your own one-sentence summary gives you a standard against which to test each choice.

questions.question: A passage examines three factors affecting yield and shows pH mattered most. Which is the main idea?
options: Of the three factors studied, pH proved most influential
questions.explanation: This covers the whole passage; the first choice is too narrow and the second too broad.

lessons.title: 3.2 Supporting Details
lessons.html:
📖 Supporting Details
Details exist to prove the claim — the question is which one does the proving.

Key Words & Meanings

Tap a word to open its definition.

supporting detail

A fact, reason, example, or statistic that develops a central idea.

evidence

Information used to support a conclusion.

relevance

A direct connection between evidence and the claim.

citation

A reference to information taken from a source.

A supporting-detail question gives you a claim and asks which piece of evidence from the passage backs it. These are the fastest points in Reading & Writing because the answer is printed in front of you; the skill is matching precisely rather than approximately.

The Digital SAT also asks the reverse: it presents four pieces of data or quotation and asks which would most effectively support a stated conclusion. Here the correct answer must match the conclusion's exact terms, not merely its topic.

Key points

  • Locate the claim first, then hunt for evidence — never the other way round.
  • The right evidence matches the claim's specific terms, not just its subject.
  • Evidence about a different group, period or measure is wrong however true it sounds.
  • If the claim is comparative, the evidence must compare.
  • If the claim is causal, evidence of correlation alone is insufficient.
  • You should be able to point at the exact words that do the supporting.

Example

Claim: “Rainfall in the north exceeded the southern average.” The supporting choice must give figures for both regions. A choice giving only northern rainfall, however precise, cannot support a comparison.

Why this matters

Command-of-evidence is one of the largest question groups on the test, and unlike inference it has an answer you can literally point to — making it the most reliable place to gain marks.

lessons.title: 📝 Practice: Supporting Details
lessons.html: Quick check: Review the lesson notes and work the two practice questions, then answer these to confirm you understood Supporting Details.

questions.question: A claim compares rainfall in two regions. Which evidence supports it?
options: Precise figures for the northern region only
questions.explanation: A comparative claim requires comparative evidence; data from one region alone cannot establish it.

questions.question: What is the correct order of work on a supporting-detail question?
options: Read the choices, then find the claim
Find the claim, then hunt for evidence
Read the whole passage twice first
questions.explanation: Identifying exactly what must be supported tells you what to look for among the choices.

questions.question: Why can correlation evidence fail to support a causal claim?
options: Correlations only apply to small samples
A correlation can arise without one thing causing the other
questions.explanation: Two things can move together for other reasons, so correlation alone does not establish causation.

lessons.title: 3.3 Making Inferences
lessons.html:
📖 Making Inferences
One logical step from the text — never two, and never from your own knowledge.

Key Words & Meanings

Tap a word to open its definition.

inference

A logical conclusion supported by textual evidence but not stated directly.

imply

To suggest an idea without saying it explicitly.

assumption

An unstated belief that may lack adequate evidence.

logical support

Evidence and reasoning that justify a conclusion.

An inference is a conclusion the passage strongly supports without stating outright. The stem usually says suggests, implies, indicates, or asks which choice most logically completes the text.

The correct answer is always one short step from something printed. Wrong answers fall into three families: they take two steps, they import outside knowledge, or they overstate a qualified claim into an absolute one.

Key points

  • The answer must be supported by the text and by nothing else.
  • One step only. If you need a second assumption, it is the wrong choice.
  • Reject absolutes — always, never, all, only, must — unless the passage is that strong.
  • Reject anything true in the world but absent from the passage.
  • For “most logically completes”, read the sentence before the blank for the logical direction.
  • Prove your choice: name the words that force it.

Example

Passage: “Although the clinic opened in 2015, no vaccination records exist before 2018.” Inference: records were not kept in those first years. Not “the clinic was closed” — that contradicts the text — and not “funding was withdrawn”, which the passage never mentions.

Why this matters

Inference questions are where strong readers most often talk themselves out of a correct answer. The discipline of pointing at supporting words is what makes them consistent.

lessons.title: 📝 Practice: Making Inferences
lessons.html: Quick check: Review the lesson notes and work the two practice questions, then answer these to confirm you understood Making Inferences.

questions.question: 'Although the clinic opened in 2015, no vaccination records exist before 2018.' What can be inferred?
options: Records were not kept in the clinic's first years
questions.explanation: The absence of records is one step from the text; the other choices contradict it or import information.

questions.question: How far from the stated text should a correct inference be?
options: As far as general knowledge allows
It need not relate to the text
questions.explanation: SAT inferences are always one supported step from the passage, never a chain of assumptions.

questions.question: Why are absolute words often wrong in inference choices?
options: They make the option too long
Passages usually make qualified claims that absolutes overstate
They appear only in wrong answers by rule
questions.explanation: Overstating a qualified claim into an absolute is a standard trap in inference answer choices.

lessons.title: 3.4 Interpreting Data and Graphs
lessons.html:
📖 Interpreting Data and Graphs
Read the axes before you read the choices.

Key Words & Meanings

Tap a word to open its definition.

data interpretation

The process of understanding values, patterns, and relationships in data.

axis

A reference line on a graph showing a variable and scale.

trend

A general direction of change across values.

outlier

A value noticeably different from the rest of a dataset.

Reading & Writing includes questions pairing a short passage with a table, bar chart, line graph or scatterplot. You are usually asked which choice accurately describes the data, or which completes a claim consistently with the graphic.

No mathematics is required. What is required is care: read the title, both axis labels, the units and the legend before looking at the answers. Most wrong choices are wrong because they mix up a unit, a category or a direction.

Key points

  • Read title, axis labels, units and legend first.
  • Check whether values are counts, percentages or rates — they are not interchangeable.
  • A rising percentage can accompany a falling count if the total shrank.
  • Answer only from the graphic; do not add what the passage implies unless asked to combine them.
  • Watch direction words: increased, exceeded, fewer than, at least.
  • When a claim must be consistent with the data, verify the numbers, not the wording.

Example

A bar chart shows cassava output in tonnes; a choice describes the change “by 15 percent”. Unless the chart shows percentages, that choice cannot be verified from it and is wrong — even if 15 percent happens to be arithmetically correct.

Why this matters

Data questions appear in both modules of Reading & Writing and are pure accuracy. They reward slow reading of the labels far more than any reasoning skill.

options: The final sentence of the passage
The title, axis labels, units and legend
questions.explanation: Most wrong answers confuse a unit, category or direction, all of which the labels settle immediately.

options: Unverifiable from the chart, so wrong
Correct because percentages are always valid

lessons.title: 3.5 Evidence-Based Questions
lessons.html:
📖 Evidence-Based Questions
The SAT wants the evidence that does the work, not the evidence that sounds impressive.

Key Words & Meanings

Tap a word to open its definition.

evidence-based question

A question requiring textual or quantitative proof for a conclusion.

claim

A statement presented for acceptance or evaluation.

quotation

Exact words taken from a source.

corroborate

To strengthen a claim with additional evidence.

Command-of-evidence questions come in two forms. Textual evidence asks which quotation best supports a claim. Quantitative evidence asks which data point from a table or graph does. Both test the same thing: precision of match.

The test frequently offers evidence that is genuinely relevant to the topic but does not support the specific claim being made. Relevance is not support — the evidence must address the claim's exact terms.

Key points

  • Restate the claim in your own words before examining the choices.
  • Ask of each choice: does this make the claim more likely to be true?
  • Relevant to the topic is not the same as supporting the claim.
  • For a hypothesis, the right evidence usually confirms its specific prediction.
  • For quantitative items, verify the numbers against the graphic rather than trusting the wording.
  • If two choices seem to support the claim, one addresses it more directly — find which.

Example

A researcher hypothesises that shade increases seedling survival. The supporting choice must compare shaded and unshaded survival rates. A choice reporting that shaded seedlings grew taller is relevant, interesting, and does not test the hypothesis.

Why this matters

Command-of-evidence is among the most heavily represented question types on the Digital SAT. Because the answer is verifiable rather than interpretive, method reliably beats intuition here.

lessons.title: 📝 Practice: Evidence-Based Questions
lessons.html: Quick check: Review the lesson notes and work the two practice questions, then answer these to confirm you understood Evidence-Based Questions.

questions.question: A hypothesis says shade increases seedling survival. Which finding best supports it?
options: More seedlings were planted in shade
Survival was higher among shaded than unshaded seedlings
questions.explanation: The evidence must test the hypothesis's specific prediction about survival, not a related but different outcome.

questions.question: What is the difference between relevant and supporting evidence?
options: Relevant evidence concerns the topic; supporting evidence makes the specific claim more likely
questions.explanation: The SAT frequently offers topically relevant choices that do not address the claim actually being made.

questions.question: For a quantitative evidence question, what should you verify?
options: The numbers against the graphic itself
That the choice mentions the passage
questions.explanation: Quantitative choices must be checked against the data displayed, since wording alone can misdescribe it.

lessons.title: 3.6 Text Analysis
lessons.html:
📖 Text Analysis
Ask what the passage is doing, not only what it says.

Key Words & Meanings

Tap a word to open its definition.

text analysis

Close examination of how a text's ideas, language, and structure create meaning.

rhetorical function

The job performed by a sentence or passage.

context

Information surrounding a statement that shapes its meaning.

interpretation

An evidence-supported explanation of meaning.

Text-analysis questions ask about function: why a sentence is there, how a paragraph is built, what role an example plays. The content matters less than the job each part performs.

Useful labels: a sentence may introduce, define, illustrate, qualify, contrast, concede, or conclude. Naming the job before reading the options makes the right choice obvious.

Key points

  • Ask why is this sentence here? rather than what does it say?
  • Common jobs: introduce, define, illustrate, qualify, contrast, concede, conclude.
  • An example never proves a claim on the SAT — it illustrates it.
  • A concession (admittedly, granted) strengthens the argument that follows it.
  • Choices describing the content correctly but the function wrongly are the standard trap.

Example

A passage argues rice yields can rise, then adds: “Admittedly, three seasons of data is a short record.” Its function is to acknowledge a limitation, not to reject the argument. A choice saying it “refutes the earlier claim” misreads the job entirely.

Why this matters

Function questions look subjective and are not. Once you name the job in your own words, the correct option usually matches it almost word for word.

lessons.title: 📝 Practice: Text Analysis
lessons.html: Quick check: Review the lesson notes and work the two practice questions, then answer these to confirm you understood Text Analysis.

questions.question: A passage argues yields can rise, then says 'Admittedly, three seasons is a short record.' This sentence:
options: Acknowledges a limitation of the evidence
questions.explanation: 'Admittedly' signals a concession, which acknowledges a weakness without abandoning the argument.

questions.question: What does a text-analysis question primarily ask about?
options: The function a sentence or paragraph performs
questions.explanation: These questions test what a portion of the text is doing within the passage's structure.

questions.question: On the SAT, what does an example do for a claim?
questions.explanation: Examples illustrate claims; choices asserting that an example proves a claim overstate its function.

Key Words & Meanings

Tap a word to open its definition.

guided practice

Supported application of a newly learned skill.

worked solution

A step-by-step explanation of how an answer is reached.

error analysis

Review of why an answer was wrong and how to correct the method.

transfer

Application of a learned skill to a new problem.

This lesson consolidates Module 3. Every question here is answerable from a short passage or a graphic, and every correct answer can be pointed at. Work through them untimed first, then repeat at about 70 seconds per question.

Mark each attempt with the reason for any error: too narrow, too broad, outside knowledge, misread unit, or overstated absolute. Those five labels cover almost every mistake made in this module.

Key points

  • Main idea — whole passage, not one sentence.
  • Supporting detail — the evidence must match the claim's exact terms.
  • Inference — one step from the text, nothing imported.
  • Data — read title, axes, units and legend before the choices.
  • Log every error by reason, not by topic.

Example

After ten practice questions a student finds six errors: four too narrow and two misread unit. That is not a reading problem, it is two habits. The next session drills summarising before looking at choices, and reading axis labels aloud.

Why this matters

Practice only improves a score when it is reviewed. Sorting errors by reason turns a score out of ten into a specific plan for the next session.

lessons.title: 4.1 Vocabulary in Context
lessons.html:
📖 Vocabulary in Context
The sentence decides the meaning, not the dictionary.

Key Words & Meanings

Tap a word to open its definition.

contextual meaning

The meaning a word has in a particular sentence or passage.

connotation

A feeling or association connected to a word.

substitution

Replacing one expression with another to test meaning.

precision

Exactness in meaning and word choice.

These questions give a short passage with a blank or an underlined word and ask which choice best fits the meaning as used. Many tested words are common words carrying an academic sense.

Cover the choices. Read the sentence and put your own simple word in the gap. Then find the choice closest to your word. Doing it in this order stops the familiar-but-wrong option from capturing you.

Key points

  • Predict your own word before reading the four choices.
  • The common meaning of a word is usually the trap, not the answer.
  • Match the sentence's charge: positive, negative or neutral.
  • Substitute your chosen word back in and re-read the whole sentence.
  • If two choices both fit loosely, one fits the register of academic writing better.

Example

“The findings qualify earlier conclusions about migration.” Not “make eligible”, the common meaning. Here it means limit or moderate. Predicting “soften” or “restrict” leads you straight to it.

Why this matters

Vocabulary in context appears several times in every module, and because it rewards a repeatable method rather than a memorised list, it is one of the fastest areas to improve.

lessons.title: 4.2 Author's Purpose
lessons.html:
📖 Author's Purpose
Every passage is written to do something: inform, argue, describe, or persuade.

Key Words & Meanings

Tap a word to open its definition.

author's purpose

The reason an author creates a text or includes a particular element.

rhetorical function

The role a sentence or detail performs.

audience

The intended readers of a text.

qualification

A limit or condition added to make a claim more accurate.

Purpose questions ask why the author wrote the passage or a particular part of it. The four broad purposes are to inform, to argue, to describe and to persuade, and the wording of the passage usually announces which.

Neutral, factual language signals informing. Evaluative language — should, must, fails to, compelling — signals arguing or persuading. Sensory and concrete language signals describing.

Key points

  • Neutral factual language → informing.
  • Evaluative or prescriptive language → arguing or persuading.
  • Concrete, sensory language → describing.
  • A purpose choice must cover the whole passage, not one striking sentence.
  • Watch verbs in the choices: refute, illustrate, summarise and advocate are not interchangeable.

Example

A passage lists three irrigation methods with their costs and yields, using no evaluative language. Its purpose is to inform or compare. A choice saying it “advocates drip irrigation” requires recommending language the passage never uses.

Why this matters

Purpose questions test whether you register tone as well as content, and they use the same too-narrow / too-broad logic that settles main-idea questions.

lessons.title: 4.3 Tone and Style
lessons.html:
📖 Tone and Style
Tone is the author's attitude; style is how the writing is built.

Key Words & Meanings

Tap a word to open its definition.

tone

The author's attitude toward the subject or audience.

style

The characteristic way an author uses language.

diction

The author's choice of words.

formality

The degree to which language follows conventional academic standards.

Tone is attitude toward the subject: approving, critical, sceptical, admiring, neutral, cautious. Style is the manner: formal or informal, technical or plain, dense or direct.

Academic writing on the SAT is rarely emotional. Extreme tone words — furious, ecstatic, contemptuous — are almost always wrong. The right answer is usually a measured word such as cautious, appreciative, sceptical or objective.

Key points

  • Tone = attitude; style = manner of expression.
  • Extreme emotional words are almost always the wrong choice.
  • Adjectives and adverbs carry tone; nouns and verbs mostly carry content.
  • A hedge (may, appears, suggests) signals a cautious tone.
  • In Expression of Ideas, keep the style of a revision consistent with the passage's.

Example

“The results are promising, though the sample was small and further work is needed.” The tone is cautiously optimistic — not enthusiastic, which ignores the hedging, and not dismissive, which ignores promising.

Why this matters

Tone questions are quick when you look at the modifiers rather than the subject matter, and the same instinct stops you choosing an over-formal or over-casual revision in Expression of Ideas.

lessons.title: 4.4 Comparing Passages
lessons.html:
📖 Comparing Passages
Two texts, one question: where exactly do they disagree?

Key Words & Meanings

Tap a word to open its definition.

paired texts

Two passages examined together because their ideas are related.

agreement

A point on which authors share a position.

contrast

A meaningful difference between ideas or methods.

perspective

A particular viewpoint from which a subject is understood.

Paired-passage questions give two short texts on the same subject and ask how the second relates to the first. The usual relationships are agreement, disagreement, qualification, or applying the first idea to a new case.

Summarise each text's position in your own words before reading the choices. Most trap answers describe one text correctly and the other wrongly, so check both halves of every option.

Key points

  • Summarise each text separately before comparing them.
  • Common relationships: agrees, disagrees, qualifies, extends, applies.
  • Check both halves of a choice — one half is often deliberately wrong.
  • Disagreement is usually about a specific point, not the whole subject.
  • Watch for a second text that accepts the finding but rejects the explanation.

Example

Text 1 argues drought caused a yield fall. Text 2 accepts the fall but attributes it to poor seed. They agree on the fact and disagree on the cause — a choice saying “Text 2 disputes Text 1's data” is wrong.

Why this matters

Paired passages look like double the work and are not, provided you fix each position in your own words first. The comparison then takes seconds.

lessons.title: 4.5 Text Structure
lessons.html:
📖 Text Structure
How a passage is organised is itself a testable fact.

Key Words & Meanings

Tap a word to open its definition.

text structure

The organizational pattern used to arrange ideas.

chronology

Organization according to time order.

cause and effect

A structure explaining why something happens and what follows.

problem and solution

A structure presenting a difficulty and a response.

Structure questions ask how a passage is arranged: problem then solution, claim then evidence, chronological, general then specific, cause then effect, or comparison. Short SAT passages usually follow one clean pattern.

Read the first and last sentences and ask what changed between them. That movement — from question to answer, from general to particular, from past to present — is the structure.

Key points

  • Common patterns: problem/solution, claim/evidence, chronological, general/specific, cause/effect, compare/contrast.
  • Compare the first and last sentences to see the movement.
  • Signal words mark the pattern: first, then, however, as a result, for instance.
  • A choice must describe the whole arrangement, not one transition inside it.
  • In Expression of Ideas, structure decides where a new sentence should be inserted.

Example

A passage opens with falling fish stocks and closes with a proposed quota system. The structure is problem then solution. A choice calling it “a chronological account” describes the surface, not the arrangement.

Why this matters

Recognising structure answers structure questions directly and also tells you where an inserted sentence belongs — a common Expression of Ideas task.

lessons.title: 4.6 Analyzing Arguments
lessons.html:
📖 Analyzing Arguments
Find the conclusion first; everything else is either support for it or noise.

Key Words & Meanings

Tap a word to open its definition.

argument

A claim supported by evidence and reasoning.

premise

A reason or statement offered in support of a conclusion.

validity

The quality of reasoning in which a conclusion follows logically.

counterargument

A reasoned position opposing the main claim.

An argument has a conclusion (what the author wants you to accept), premises (the reasons given), and assumptions (unstated links the reasoning depends on).

Locate the conclusion by asking what the passage is trying to convince you of. Words such as therefore, thus, so, it follows that mark it, but often it simply sits in the last sentence.

Key points

  • Conclusion = the claim being urged; premises = the reasons offered.
  • An assumption is unstated and necessary — remove it and the argument collapses.
  • To weaken: attack the assumption or supply an alternative explanation.
  • To strengthen: rule out an alternative explanation.
  • A conclusion drawn from a small or unrepresentative sample is vulnerable to that fact.

Example

Argument: “Schools with libraries score higher, so building libraries will raise scores.” The assumption is that the library causes the difference. Noting that such schools are also better funded overall weakens it by supplying another explanation.

Why this matters

Argument questions appear throughout Reading & Writing and reappear in Craft and Structure. The conclusion/premise/assumption split handles nearly all of them.

questions.explanation: An alternative explanation undermines the causal link the argument depends on.

questions.explanation: Short argumentative passages usually build to the conclusion, placing it in the final sentence.

Key Words & Meanings

Tap a word to open its definition.

mixed practice

Exercises combining several skills in one set.

justification

A clear reason supported by evidence.

distractor pattern

A recurring way an incorrect option misleads test takers.

reflection

Deliberate review of performance to improve future decisions.

This lesson consolidates Module 4. These questions reward naming things before choosing: name the word you expect, the purpose, the tone, the structure, or the conclusion — then match a choice to your name.

Work untimed first, then repeat at about 70 seconds per question. Log errors by reason, not by topic.

  • Vocabulary — predict your own word first.

  • Tone — look at adjectives and adverbs, and avoid extremes.
  • Structure — compare first and last sentences.
  • Arguments — find the conclusion, then the assumption holding it up.

Example

A student misses four questions: two tone (both chose an extreme word) and two purpose (both chose “advocates” for informative passages). One habit fixes both — check the modifiers before choosing.

Why this matters

Module 4 questions look interpretive but are decided by textual signals. Practising the naming step is what converts them from guesswork into method.

lessons.title: 5.1 Improving Sentences
lessons.html:
📖 Improving Sentences
Between two correct options, the SAT always prefers the shorter one.

Key Words & Meanings

Tap a word to open its definition.

revision

A change that improves meaning, organization, or language.

conciseness

Clear expression without unnecessary words.

redundancy

Needless repetition of the same idea.

clarity

The quality of being easy to understand.

These questions offer four versions of a sentence and ask which is best. First eliminate anything grammatically wrong. Among what survives, choose the version that is clearest and most concise.

The SAT dislikes redundancy (“annual yearly report”), wordiness (“due to the fact that” for because), and passive voice where an active sentence would do.

Key points

  • Eliminate grammatical errors first, then judge concision.
  • Cut redundancy: free gift, past history, annual yearly.
  • Replace wordy phrases: due to the fact that → because.
  • Prefer active voice unless the doer is genuinely unimportant.
  • Never change the meaning to make a sentence shorter.

Example

“Due to the fact that the rains were late, the harvest was, as a result, poor.” Two wordy phrases and a doubled causal link. Better: “Because the rains were late, the harvest was poor.”

Why this matters

Concision questions are quick and rule-driven. Once you know the SAT's preference, the shortest grammatical option is right often enough to be a reliable tie-breaker.

lessons.title: 5.2 Organization of Paragraphs
lessons.html:
📖 Organization of Paragraphs
One idea per paragraph, announced in the first sentence.

Key Words & Meanings

Tap a word to open its definition.

paragraph organization

The logical arrangement of sentences around one controlling idea.

topic sentence

A sentence stating a paragraph's main point.

unity

The quality of every sentence supporting the same focus.

development

Supporting a central idea with sufficient explanation and evidence.

Organisation questions ask where a sentence belongs, which sentence should open a paragraph, or whether a sentence should be kept or removed. All three depend on one principle: a paragraph develops a single idea.

A topic sentence states that idea. Every other sentence in the paragraph must serve it. A sentence that introduces a different subject belongs elsewhere — or nowhere.

Key points

  • Each paragraph develops one idea, stated in its topic sentence.
  • To place a sentence, find the paragraph whose idea it serves.
  • Pronouns and this/these point backwards — use them to locate position.
  • A sentence that changes the subject should be removed, however interesting.
  • Chronological or logical order within a paragraph is rarely accidental.

Example

A paragraph about irrigation costs contains a sentence about pest resistance. Interesting, well written, and off-topic — the SAT's answer is to remove it, because it does not serve the paragraph's single idea.

Why this matters

Organisation questions are decided by a rule rather than by taste, and the same one-idea principle answers insert, order and delete questions alike.

lessons.title: 5.3 Logical Flow
lessons.html:
📖 Logical Flow
Ideas must arrive in an order the reader can follow without backtracking.

Key Words & Meanings

Tap a word to open its definition.

logical flow

The clear, reasonable progression of ideas.

coherence

The overall logical connection among ideas.

transition

A word or phrase showing an idea relationship.

sequence

The order in which information is presented.

Flow questions test sequence: does this sentence follow from the last one, and does the next follow from it? Problems appear when an idea arrives before the information needed to understand it.

The most reliable check is to read the sentence before the blank and the sentence after it, ignoring everything else. The gap between those two is what the answer must bridge.

Key points

  • Read only the sentence before and the sentence after the blank.
  • A term must be introduced before it is discussed.
  • General statements normally precede their specific examples.
  • Cause precedes effect unless a transition signals otherwise.
  • If a choice repeats what has just been said, it adds nothing and is wrong.

Example

A paragraph mentions “this technique” in its second sentence, but no technique has been named. The missing first sentence must introduce the technique — not describe its results, which the paragraph goes on to do anyway.

Why this matters

Flow questions are quick once you stop re-reading the whole paragraph. The two neighbouring sentences contain everything the answer must satisfy.

lessons.title: 5.4 Combining Sentences
lessons.html:
📖 Combining Sentences
The right join is the one that shows the true relationship between the two ideas.

Key Words & Meanings

Tap a word to open its definition.

coordination

Joining grammatically equal ideas.

subordination

Making one idea dependent on a more important idea.

relative clause

A clause beginning with who, which, or that and describing a noun.

sentence boundary

The punctuation or conjunction separating complete clauses.

Sentence-combining questions give you two short sentences and ask for the most effective single sentence. The best answer keeps all the information, removes repetition, and makes the logical relationship explicit.

Choose the joining method by relationship: a relative clause for added description, a subordinator for cause or contrast, a coordinating conjunction for equal weight, an appositive for renaming.

Key points

  • Keep every piece of information; losing one makes a choice wrong.
  • Relative clause (which, who) — adds description.
  • Subordinator (because, although, while) — shows cause or contrast.
  • Appositive — renames a noun: Musu, a rice farmer, ...
  • Prefer the version that is both complete and shortest.

Example

“Musu farms rice. She has worked the same plot for twenty years.” Combined with an appositive-style relative clause: “Musu, who has farmed the same rice plot for twenty years, ...” — one sentence, nothing lost, repetition removed.

Why this matters

Combining questions test the same clause knowledge as punctuation questions, so learning one strengthens the other.

questions.explanation: Relative clauses beginning with 'who' or 'which' attach description to a noun.

questions.explanation: The combination must preserve all the original information; concision never justifies losing content.

questions.question: Which structure renames a noun?
questions.explanation: An appositive is a noun phrase placed beside another noun to rename or identify it.

lessons.title: 5.5 Revising Text
lessons.html:
📖 Revising Text
Every revision question has a stated goal — answer that goal, not your own taste.

Key Words & Meanings

Tap a word to open its definition.

text revision

Improving a draft's ideas, evidence, organization, and language.

relevance

Direct connection to the text's purpose.

reordering

Moving information to create clearer progression.

synthesis

Combining information into a coherent whole.

Revision questions usually name their purpose: “which choice most effectively emphasises the study's limitations?” The correct answer is the one that achieves that stated goal, even if another option is better written.

Underline the goal in the question before reading the choices. Then test each option against it alone. A beautifully phrased choice that does not meet the goal is wrong.

Key points

  • Find and hold the stated goal in the question stem.
  • Test each choice against the goal, not against style.
  • A choice may be well written and still fail the goal — that is the standard trap.
  • If the goal is to emphasise, the answer must be specific and pointed.
  • If the goal is to introduce, the answer must be general enough to open the topic.

Example

Goal: “emphasise how quickly the flooding spread”. “The water rose across four districts within six hours” meets it. “The flooding caused considerable disruption” is true, fluent, and says nothing about speed.

Why this matters

Goal-directed revision questions are common in Expression of Ideas and are among the easiest to get wrong by answering a question that was not asked.

lessons.title: 5.6 Practice Questions
lessons.html:
📖 Practice Questions
Practice for Expression of Ideas: concision, organisation, flow, goals.

Key Words & Meanings

Tap a word to open its definition.

practice question

A learning item used to apply a tested skill before formal assessment.

rationale

The reason an answer is correct or incorrect.

error log

A record of mistakes, causes, and corrections.

transfer

Use of a learned method in a new context.

This lesson consolidates Module 5. Expression of Ideas questions almost always have a stated goal or a structural rule behind them, so the work is to identify which one applies before comparing choices.

Do these untimed first, then at about 70 seconds each. Record every error as one of: missed the stated goal, kept redundancy, broke paragraph unity, or misjudged flow.

Key points

  • Concision — shortest grammatical version that keeps the meaning.
  • Organisation — one idea per paragraph.
  • Flow — the two neighbouring sentences define the gap.
  • Goals — answer the question actually asked.
  • Log errors by reason so the next session has a target.

Example

A student misses three: all three were goal questions where a fluent but off-goal choice won. The fix is mechanical — underline the goal before looking at any option.

Why this matters

Expression of Ideas is the most improvable part of Reading & Writing because almost every question is decided by a rule you can learn rather than by reading ability.

lessons.title: 6.1 Subject-Verb Agreement
lessons.html:
📖 Subject-Verb Agreement
Find the subject, ignore everything between it and the verb.

Key Words & Meanings

Tap a word to open its definition.

subject-verb agreement

The grammatical matching of a subject and verb in number.

subject

The noun or pronoun a clause is about.

intervening phrase

Words between a subject and verb that do not control agreement.

collective noun

A singular noun naming a group.

A verb agrees with its subject in number. The SAT hides the subject by inserting phrases between it and the verb, so the noun nearest the verb is usually the wrong one to match.

Cross out prepositional phrases (of the documents, in the villages) and clauses set off by commas. What remains beside the verb is the subject.

Key points

  • Cross out phrases between the subject and the verb before deciding.
  • Each, every, either, neither, one, none take a singular verb.
  • Compound subjects joined by and are plural.
  • With or / nor, the verb agrees with the nearer subject.
  • In there is / there are, the subject follows the verb.
  • Collective nouns (team, committee) usually take a singular verb.

Example

“Each of the twelve districts ___ submitted a report.” Cross out of the twelve districts: the subject is Each, singular, so has. The plural districts sitting next to the verb is the trap.

Why this matters

Agreement is one of the most frequently tested conventions and one of the easiest to secure, because the crossing-out method works every time.

questions.explanation: 'Each' is the singular subject; the intervening prepositional phrase does not affect agreement.

questions.explanation: With 'or' and 'nor', the verb matches whichever subject is closer to it.
