lessons.title: 6.2 Verb Tenses
lessons.html:
📖 Verb Tenses
Keep the tense the passage has already established unless meaning demands a change.

Key Words & Meanings

Tap a word to open its definition.

verb tense

A verb form locating an action or state in time.

aspect

A form showing whether an action is ongoing or completed.

tense shift

A change in verb time, correct only when meaning requires it.

past participle

A verb form used with have or be.

Most tense questions test consistency: a passage written in the past stays in the past. Look at the verbs in the surrounding sentences and match them.

The perfect tenses appear when one action precedes another. Use the past perfect (had studied) for the earlier of two past actions, and the present perfect (has studied) for something begun in the past and still relevant now.

Key points

  • Match the tense already established in the surrounding sentences.
  • Past perfect (had done) marks the earlier of two past events.
  • Present perfect (has done) links past action to the present.
  • A time marker (in 1998, since 2010, currently) fixes the required tense.
  • Do not shift tense mid-sentence without a reason in the meaning.
  • Scientific findings and permanent truths take the present tense.

Example

“By the time the survey began, the clinic ___ operating for three years.” Two past events, and the operating came first, so the past perfect: had been.

Why this matters

Tense questions are settled by evidence inside the passage — the surrounding verbs and any time marker — so they never require guessing.

lessons.html: Quick check: Review the lesson notes and work the two practice questions, then answer these to confirm you understood Verb Tenses.

questions.explanation: The past perfect marks the earlier of two past events, here the operating that preceded the survey.

questions.question: What most often decides the correct tense on the SAT?
options: The tense already used in surrounding sentences
The first word of the paragraph

questions.question: Which tense links a past action to the present?
questions.explanation: The present perfect, 'has/have done', connects a past action to its present relevance.

lessons.title: 6.3 Pronouns
lessons.html:
📖 Pronouns
A pronoun needs a clear, singular-or-plural-matching antecedent.

Key Words & Meanings

Tap a word to open its definition.

pronoun

A word used in place of a noun or noun phrase.

antecedent

The noun or phrase to which a pronoun refers.

agreement

The matching of a pronoun and antecedent.

ambiguity

Uncertainty caused when a pronoun could refer to more than one noun.

Pronoun questions test three things: agreement in number with the noun replaced, case (subject or object), and clarity of reference.

Ambiguity is the subtlest of the three. If a pronoun could refer to two different nouns, the SAT treats the sentence as wrong even though it is grammatical.

Key points

  • A pronoun matches its antecedent in number: a singular noun takes it, not they.
  • Subject case: I, he, she, we, they, who. Object case: me, him, her, us, them, whom.
  • Test who/whom by substituting he/him: if him fits, use whom.
  • If a pronoun could point to two nouns, the reference is ambiguous and wrong.
  • Its is possessive; it's means it is.
  • Their with a singular indefinite pronoun is not accepted on the SAT.

Example

“When the committee met the researchers, they presented the findings.” Who presented — committee or researchers? The pronoun is ambiguous, so the sentence must be rewritten to name the group.

Why this matters

Pronoun errors are common in every module and are easy to miss because ambiguous sentences read perfectly well aloud.

options: Substitute 'he' or 'him' and see which fits

options: Her and the team arrived late.
Between you and I, the plan is sound.
Between you and me, the plan is sound.
Him and I reviewed the report.
questions.explanation: 'Between' is a preposition and takes object pronouns, so 'you and me' is correct.

lessons.title: 6.4 Modifiers
lessons.html:
📖 Modifiers
A modifier attaches to whatever sits next to it — make sure that is the right thing.

Key Words & Meanings

Tap a word to open its definition.

modifier

A word, phrase, or clause that describes another element.

dangling modifier

A modifier whose intended subject is missing.

misplaced modifier

A modifier positioned so that it appears to describe the wrong word.

adverbial phrase

A phrase describing how, when, where, or why.

A misplaced modifier sits beside the wrong word. A dangling modifier has nothing in the sentence to attach to at all. Both produce sentences that are grammatically parseable and factually absurd.

The test: when a sentence opens with a descriptive phrase followed by a comma, the noun immediately after the comma must be the thing that phrase describes.

Key points

  • An opening descriptive phrase describes the noun right after the comma.
  • A dangling modifier has no noun in the sentence to attach to.
  • Place limiting words (only, almost, just) directly before what they limit.
  • Move the modifier, or change the subject — either can fix the sentence.
  • Read the resulting sentence literally; if it is absurd, the modifier is wrong.

Example

“Walking through the market, the prices seemed high.” Literally, the prices are walking. Fix by supplying the right subject: “Walking through the market, I found the prices high.”

Why this matters

Modifier questions are among the most reliably identifiable on the test: the opening-phrase-plus-comma pattern tells you exactly what to check.

lessons.html: Quick check: Review the lesson notes and work the two practice questions, then answer these to confirm you understood Modifiers.

options: The modifier dangles: the prices are not walking
questions.explanation: The opening phrase must describe the noun after the comma, and prices cannot walk.

questions.question: Where should the word 'only' be placed?
options: At the end of the sentence
At the start of the sentence
questions.explanation: Limiting words change meaning depending on position, so they belong beside the element they limit.

questions.question: A sentence opens with a descriptive phrase and a comma. What must follow the comma?
questions.explanation: The noun immediately after the comma is what the opening modifier attaches to.

lessons.title: 6.5 Parallel Structure
lessons.html:
📖 Parallel Structure
Items in a list or comparison must share the same grammatical form.

Key Words & Meanings

Tap a word to open its definition.

parallel structure

The use of matching grammatical forms for equal ideas.

series

Three or more items presented in a list.

correlative conjunction

A paired connector such as either...or.

comparison

A structure showing similarity or difference.

When a sentence lists items or draws a comparison, every element must take the same form: all nouns, all -ing forms, all infinitives, all clauses.

Parallelism also governs paired constructions — not only…but also, either…or, both…and. Whatever follows the first half must be matched in form by what follows the second.

Key points

  • All items in a list share one grammatical form.
  • Paired constructions must be balanced on both sides.
  • Comparisons must compare like with like, not a thing with a person's version of it.
  • Repeat the preposition or article across items if you repeat it for any of them.
  • Read the sentence stem separately with each list item to test it.

Example

“She enjoys reading, writing and to swim.” Two -ing forms and an infinitive. Correct: “reading, writing and swimming”. Likewise “The climate here is milder than Ghana” compares a climate with a country — it should be than Ghana's.

Why this matters

Parallelism appears in most Reading & Writing modules and is instantly checkable by reading the stem against each item in turn.

lessons.html: Quick check: Review the lesson notes and work the two practice questions, then answer these to confirm you understood Parallel Structure.

options: She enjoys reading, to write and swimming.

questions.explanation: All three list items must share the same form; here all are -ing forms.

options: It compares a climate with a country rather than with Ghana's climate
questions.explanation: Comparisons must compare like with like, so it should read 'than Ghana's'.

questions.question: Which construction requires balanced forms on both sides?
questions.explanation: Paired constructions such as 'not only ... but also' must be matched grammatically on each side.

lessons.title: 6.6 Punctuation
lessons.html:
📖 Punctuation
The mark you need is decided by what sits on each side of it.

Key Words & Meanings

Tap a word to open its definition.

independent clause

A clause that can stand as a complete sentence.

comma splice

Two independent clauses joined incorrectly with only a comma.

semicolon

A mark joining closely related independent clauses.

colon

A mark introducing an explanation or list after a complete clause.

Module 2 introduced the four marks; this lesson applies them under exam conditions. The single question to ask at every punctuation decision is whether each side of the mark could stand alone as a sentence.

The SAT also tests no punctuation as an answer. When no rule requires a mark, inserting one is an error — particularly between a subject and its verb, or between a verb and its object.

Key points

  • Independent + independent → period, semicolon, or comma + FANBOYS.
  • Dependent first → comma after it. Dependent last → usually no comma.
  • Colon after a complete sentence only, introducing an explanation or list.
  • Dashes in matched pairs when they enclose an interruption.
  • Never place a single comma between a subject and its verb.
  • If no rule requires a mark, the answer with no mark is correct.

Example

“The farmers who attended the training ___ reported higher yields.” The clause is essential and no rule calls for a mark, so the answer is no punctuation. A comma here would cut the subject from its verb.

Why this matters

Punctuation is the largest single group within Standard English Conventions, and every question yields to the same clause test.

lessons.title: 6.7 Capitalization
lessons.html:
📖 Capitalization
Capitalise proper nouns and sentence openings — not words you think are important.

Key Words & Meanings

Tap a word to open its definition.

capitalization

The use of uppercase letters according to standard conventions.

proper noun

The specific name of a person, place, organization, or title.

common noun

A general name that normally is not capitalized.

title case

A system for capitalizing principal words in a title.

Capitalisation is lightly tested but easy to secure. Capitalise the first word of a sentence, proper nouns and adjectives formed from them, titles used before a name, and the main words of published titles.

Do not capitalise seasons, directions used generally, job titles used generically, or academic subjects other than languages.

Key points

  • Proper nouns and proper adjectives: Liberia, Liberian, Monrovia.
  • Titles before a name are capitalised: President Weah; after, generally not.
  • Seasons are lower case: the rains came late in summer.
  • Directions are lower case unless they name a region: drive north vs the North.
  • Academic subjects are lower case except languages: biology but English.
  • Do not capitalise for emphasis — the SAT never rewards it.

Example

“She studied Biology and english at the University in monrovia.” Corrected: “She studied biology and English at the university in Monrovia.” — language capitalised, subject not, place capitalised, generic noun not.

Why this matters

These questions take seconds and are decided by a short list of rules, making them among the cheapest points available.

lessons.title: 6.8 Word Choice
lessons.html:
📖 Word Choice
Commonly confused words are tested by meaning, not by sound.

Key Words & Meanings

Tap a word to open its definition.

word choice

The selection of language for exact meaning, grammar, and tone.

idiom

A conventional expression whose wording is fixed.

collocation

Words that naturally occur together.

register

The level of formality appropriate to a context.

This is the vocabulary half of the conventions questions: choosing between words that sound alike or are frequently mixed up. There is no reasoning trick, only a list worth knowing.

The SAT also tests idiom — which preposition a word takes. Different from, capable of, consists of, preferable to, concerned with. Idiom errors are invisible unless you know the pairing.

Key points

  • Affect is usually the verb; effect usually the noun.
  • Their / there / they're and your / you're — possessive, place, contraction.
  • Fewer for countable, less for uncountable.
  • Then is time; than is comparison.
  • Principal is chief or a person; principle is a rule.
  • Learn idiomatic prepositions as fixed pairs, not by logic.

Example

“The new policy will ___ yields, and its ___ will be measured next season.” The first is a verb (affect), the second a noun (effect). Sound gives no help here; only the grammatical role does.

Why this matters

Word-choice questions appear in every module, cost nothing in time, and are pure knowledge — which makes them the most efficient thing to revise the week before the test.

questions.explanation: 'Affect' is the verb meaning to influence; 'effect' is the noun meaning result.

questions.explanation: Standard written English on the SAT uses 'different from'.

options: The yield was higher then last year.

lessons.title: 6.9 Common Grammar Errors
lessons.html:
📖 Common Grammar Errors
A short checklist catches most of what the SAT actually tests.

Key Words & Meanings

Tap a word to open its definition.

grammar error

A form that violates standard sentence conventions.

sentence fragment

An incomplete clause presented as a sentence.

run-on sentence

Independent clauses joined without correct punctuation.

error pattern

A type of mistake that occurs repeatedly.

Standard English Conventions is drawn from a small, predictable set. Knowing the list means you can scan an underlined portion and ask the right question immediately rather than reading for what “sounds wrong”.

Sounding wrong is unreliable: many correct SAT sentences sound stiff, and several classic errors — comma splices, ambiguous pronouns, dangling modifiers — sound perfectly natural when read aloud.

Key points

  • Comma splice — two independent clauses joined by a comma alone.
  • Subject–verb disagreement hidden behind an intervening phrase.
  • Ambiguous or number-mismatched pronoun.
  • Dangling or misplaced modifier after an opening phrase.
  • Faulty parallelism in a list or comparison.
  • Redundancy and wordiness where a shorter version exists.

Example

“The report was thorough, it covered every district.” This reads naturally and is a comma splice. Correct it with a semicolon, a period, or “thorough, and it covered”.

Why this matters

Roughly a quarter of Reading & Writing is conventions, and this list covers most of it. Learning it converts a section that feels like intuition into one that follows rules.

questions.explanation: The SAT does not test spelling; the other three are core Standard English Conventions errors.

lessons.title: 7.1 Numbers and Operations
lessons.html:
📖 Numbers and Operations
Order of operations and sign rules underlie every Math question you will meet.

Key Words & Meanings

Tap a word to open its definition.

Numbers and Operations

Rules and properties for calculating with real numbers.

variable

A symbol representing an unknown or changing quantity.

equation

A statement that two mathematical expressions have equal value.

verification

Checking a result in the original conditions to confirm it is valid.

Arithmetic on the SAT is never the point, but arithmetic mistakes cost real points. Two rules do most of the work: order of operations and the sign rules for negatives.

Order: brackets, exponents, multiplication and division left to right, then addition and subtraction left to right. Signs: two negatives multiplied or divided give a positive; subtracting a negative adds.

Key points

  • Order of operations: brackets → exponents → × ÷ → + −, left to right.
  • Multiplication and division rank equally — work left to right, not multiplication first.
  • Negative × negative = positive; negative × positive = negative.
  • Subtracting a negative is adding: 5 − (−3) = 8.
  • An even power of a negative is positive; an odd power stays negative.
  • Integers are whole numbers including negatives; zero is even and neither positive nor negative.

Example

8 − 2 × 32. Exponent first: 32 = 9. Then multiply: 2 × 9 = 18. Then subtract: 8 − 18 = −10. Working left to right instead gives 54, which is the trap answer.

Why this matters

Every algebra, geometry and data question rests on this arithmetic. A sign slip in the last line loses the mark just as completely as not knowing the method.

lessons.title: 7.2 Fractions and Decimals
lessons.html:
📖 Fractions and Decimals
A fraction is a division waiting to happen; convert whenever it makes the work easier.

Key Words & Meanings

Tap a word to open its definition.

Fractions and Decimals

Equivalent ways to represent parts of a whole or non-integer values.

variable

A symbol representing an unknown or changing quantity.

equation

A statement that two mathematical expressions have equal value.

verification

Checking a result in the original conditions to confirm it is valid.

Adding or subtracting fractions needs a common denominator; multiplying does not. To divide by a fraction, multiply by its reciprocal.

Decimals and fractions are interchangeable, and the SAT often makes one form far easier than the other. Knowing the common conversions by heart saves calculator time.

Key points

  • Add and subtract only over a common denominator.
  • Multiply fractions straight across; divide by multiplying by the reciprocal.
  • Learn by heart: 1/2 = 0.5, 1/4 = 0.25, 3/4 = 0.75, 1/5 = 0.2, 1/8 = 0.125.
  • A fraction inside a fraction is just a division — rewrite it.
  • Simplify before multiplying; cancelling first keeps the numbers small.
  • Student-produced responses accept a fraction or a decimal, so give whichever is exact.

Example

2/3 ÷ 4/9 = 2/3 × 9/4. Cancel 3 into 9 and 2 into 4: 1/1 × 3/2 = 3/2. Cancelling first avoids multiplying 18/12 and simplifying afterwards.

Why this matters

Fraction work appears throughout Math, and in student-produced responses an unsimplified or rounded answer can be marked wrong where the exact fraction would score.

lessons.title: 7.3 Percentages
lessons.html:
📖 Percentages
Percent means per hundred, and every percent question is one of three shapes.

Key Words & Meanings

Tap a word to open its definition.

Percentages

Ratios expressed per one hundred.

variable

A symbol representing an unknown or changing quantity.

equation

A statement that two mathematical expressions have equal value.

verification

Checking a result in the original conditions to confirm it is valid.

The three shapes are: find the percent of a number, find what percent one number is of another, and find the original after a percent change. All three come from part = percent × whole.

Percent increase multiplies by (1 + rate); percent decrease multiplies by (1 − rate). Successive changes multiply — they never add.

Key points

  • part = percent × whole; rearrange for whichever is missing.
  • Increase by 20% → × 1.20. Decrease by 20% → × 0.80.
  • Successive percent changes multiply: +20% then −20% is ×1.2×0.8 = 0.96.
  • Percent change = (new − old) ÷ old × 100.
  • To reverse a percent change, divide rather than applying the opposite percent.
  • “Of” means multiply; “is” means equals.

Example

A price rises 20% then falls 20%. Not back to the start: 1.20 × 0.80 = 0.96, so it ends 4% below the original. This is the most commonly tested percent trap on the SAT.

Why this matters

Percent problems appear in Problem Solving and Data Analysis, which is a quarter of the Math section, and the multiply-not-add rule settles most of the hard ones.

questions.explanation: Percent change is (50 − 40) ÷ 40 × 100 = 25%.

lessons.title: 7.4 Ratios
lessons.html:
📖 M7:Ratios
A ratio compares parts; a fraction compares a part with the whole.

Key Words & Meanings

Tap a word to open its definition.

Ratios

Comparisons of two quantities by division.

variable

A symbol representing an unknown or changing quantity.

equation

A statement that two mathematical expressions have equal value.

verification

Checking a result in the original conditions to confirm it is valid.

A ratio a : b says how quantities compare, not how large they are. To turn a ratio into actual amounts, add the parts to find the total number of shares, then divide.

The commonest error is treating a ratio as a fraction of the whole. In a ratio of 3 : 5 there are eight shares, so the first quantity is 3/8 of the total, not 3/5.

Key points

  • Add the ratio parts to get the number of shares.
  • Part of the total = its share ÷ total shares.
  • Ratios simplify like fractions: 8 : 12 = 2 : 3.
  • Keep the order: 3 : 5 is not the same as 5 : 3.
  • To scale a ratio, multiply every part by the same number.
  • A ratio has no units of its own; the quantities it compares do.

Example

Rice and beans are planted in a ratio of 3 : 5 across 64 hectares. Shares: 3 + 5 = 8. One share = 64 ÷ 8 = 8 hectares. Rice = 3 × 8 = 24 hectares, not 3/5 of 64.

Why this matters

Ratios underpin proportions, rates and scale problems, all of which appear in Problem Solving and Data Analysis.

lessons.title: 7.5 Exponents
lessons.html:
📖 Exponents
Five rules cover almost every exponent question on the test.

Key Words & Meanings

Tap a word to open its definition.

Exponents

Notation showing repeated multiplication by a base.

variable

A symbol representing an unknown or changing quantity.

equation

A statement that two mathematical expressions have equal value.

verification

Checking a result in the original conditions to confirm it is valid.

Exponents count repeated multiplication. The SAT tests the rules for combining them far more often than it tests computing large powers.

Negative exponents mean reciprocals, and fractional exponents mean roots. Both look harder than they are once translated: x−2 = 1/x2 and x1/2 = √x.

Key points

  • Multiply same base: add exponents — xa·xb = xa+b.
  • Divide same base: subtract — xa/xb = xa−b.
  • Power of a power: multiply — (xa)b = xab.
  • x0 = 1 for any non-zero x.
  • x−n = 1/xn; x1/n = n√x.
  • Rules apply only to the same base — rewrite 4 as 22 when needed.

Example

(23)2 ÷ 24. Power of a power: 26. Divide: 26−4 = 22 = 4. Adding the exponents instead of multiplying would give 25, the standard wrong answer.

Why this matters

Exponent rules recur throughout Algebra and Advanced Math, especially in exponential functions and radical expressions.

lessons.title: 7.6 Radicals
lessons.html:
📖 M7:Radicals
A radical is a fractional exponent, which is why the exponent rules still work.

Key Words & Meanings

Tap a word to open its definition.

Radicals

Expressions containing roots, such as square roots.

variable

A symbol representing an unknown or changing quantity.

equation

A statement that two mathematical expressions have equal value.

verification

Checking a result in the original conditions to confirm it is valid.

√x means the non-negative number whose square is x. Radicals simplify by pulling out perfect-square factors: √48 = √(16·3) = 4√3.

Because √x = x1/2, every exponent rule applies. Radicals multiply and divide freely; they do not add unless the radicands match.

Key points

  • Simplify by extracting perfect-square factors.
  • √a · √b = √(ab); √a ÷ √b = √(a/b).
  • √a + √b is not √(a+b).
  • Like radicals add: 2√3 + 4√3 = 6√3.
  • √x = x1/2, so exponent rules apply.
  • Rationalise a denominator by multiplying top and bottom by the radical.

Example

√48 + √27 = 4√3 + 3√3 = 7√3. Adding under one root to get √75 is wrong — though notice √75 = 5√3, which is a different number.

Why this matters

Radicals appear in Advanced Math and in geometry through the Pythagorean theorem, where exact radical answers are frequently required.

lessons.title: 7.7 Scientific Notation
lessons.html:
📖 Scientific Notation
A compact way to write very large and very small numbers, and the SAT expects the standard form.

Key Words & Meanings

Tap a word to open its definition.

Scientific Notation

A compact form using a coefficient multiplied by a power of ten.

variable

A symbol representing an unknown or changing quantity.

equation

A statement that two mathematical expressions have equal value.

verification

Checking a result in the original conditions to confirm it is valid.

Scientific notation writes a number as a × 10n where 1 ≤ a < 10. A positive exponent means a large number, a negative exponent a small one.

To multiply, multiply the coefficients and add the exponents. To divide, divide the coefficients and subtract. Then renormalise so the coefficient sits between 1 and 10.

Key points

  • Standard form requires 1 ≤ a < 10.
  • Positive exponent → large number; negative exponent → small number.
  • Multiplying: multiply coefficients, add exponents.
  • Dividing: divide coefficients, subtract exponents.
  • Renormalise afterwards: 12 × 104 becomes 1.2 × 105.
  • Moving the decimal right decreases the exponent; moving it left increases it.

Example

(3 × 104)(4 × 103) = 12 × 107, which is not standard form. Renormalise: 1.2 × 108.

Why this matters

Scientific notation appears in science-context Math questions and in data interpretation, where large populations and small measurements are routine.

lessons.title: 7.8 Calculator Skills
lessons.html:
📖 Calculator Skills
Desmos is available for the whole Math section — knowing when not to use it matters as much as knowing how.

Key Words & Meanings

Tap a word to open its definition.

Calculator Skills

Accurate and strategic use of the built-in Desmos calculator.

variable

A symbol representing an unknown or changing quantity.

equation

A statement that two mathematical expressions have equal value.

verification

Checking a result in the original conditions to confirm it is valid.

The Bluebook app provides the Desmos graphing calculator throughout Math. It graphs equations, finds intersections and zeros, evaluates expressions and handles regressions.

It is fastest on problems that are slow by hand: solving quadratics, finding where two lines meet, reading a maximum. It is slower than your head on arithmetic, so use it selectively.

Key points

  • Type an equation and Desmos graphs it; click a point to read its coordinates.
  • Solve equations by graphing both sides and finding the intersection.
  • Find roots by graphing y = expression and reading the x-intercepts.
  • Use sliders for a parameter when a question asks how a graph changes.
  • Do not reach for it on simple arithmetic — typing costs more time than thinking.
  • Practise inside Bluebook so the interface is familiar on test day.

Example

For 2x + 5 = 3x − 4, graph y = 2x + 5 and y = 3x − 4 and read the intersection at x = 9. Faster and safer than rearranging under time pressure.

Why this matters

Candidates who practised in Desmos convert several hard questions per section into fast ones. Those meeting it for the first time on test day lose time learning it.

lessons.title: 7.9 Formula Review
lessons.html:
📖 Formula Review
Bluebook gives you a reference sheet — know what is on it and what is not.

Key Words & Meanings

Tap a word to open its definition.

Formula Review

Selection and use of equations representing mathematical relationships.

variable

A symbol representing an unknown or changing quantity.

equation

A statement that two mathematical expressions have equal value.

verification

Checking a result in the original conditions to confirm it is valid.

The Digital SAT provides a built-in reference sheet covering common geometry formulas: areas, circumference, volumes, the Pythagorean theorem and special right triangles.

It does not provide the algebra you need. Slope, the quadratic formula, percent change, averages, distance and probability all have to come from memory.

Key points

  • Provided: circle area and circumference, triangle and rectangle area, volumes, Pythagoras, special right triangles.
  • Not provided: slope = (y₂−y₁)/(x₂−x₁).
  • Not provided: quadratic formula x = (−b ± √(b²−4ac)) / 2a.
  • Not provided: percent change, mean, distance = rate × time.
  • Slope-intercept form y = mx + b and vertex form y = a(x−h)² + k.
  • Learn the short unprovided list rather than the long provided one.

Example

A student memorises circle and volume formulas — all on the reference sheet — but not the slope formula, which is not. The revision effort went entirely into what the app was going to hand him anyway.

Why this matters

Knowing which formulas the app supplies tells you exactly what to memorise, and it is a much shorter list than most candidates assume.

lessons.title: 8.1 Linear Equations
lessons.html:
📖 Linear Equations
Isolate the variable by undoing operations in reverse order.

Key Words & Meanings

Tap a word to open its definition.

Linear Equations

Equations whose variables have first power and graph as straight lines.

variable

A symbol representing an unknown or changing quantity.

equation

A statement that two mathematical expressions have equal value.

verification

Checking a result in the original conditions to confirm it is valid.

A linear equation has the variable to the first power only. Solve by doing the same thing to both sides until the variable stands alone, undoing addition before multiplication.

Linear equations are the single most common Math topic on the SAT, appearing directly and inside word problems, systems and graph questions.

Key points

  • Undo addition and subtraction first, then multiplication and division.
  • Whatever you do to one side, do to the other.
  • Distribute before collecting like terms.
  • Clear fractions by multiplying every term by the common denominator.
  • An equation reducing to 0 = 0 has infinitely many solutions; to 0 = 5, none.
  • Always substitute your answer back to check.

Example

3(x − 2) + 4 = 19. Distribute: 3x − 6 + 4 = 19. Collect: 3x − 2 = 19. Add 2: 3x = 21. Divide: x = 7. Substituting back gives 3(5) + 4 = 19. ✓

Why this matters

Linear equations are the foundation of the whole Algebra domain, which is the largest part of the Math section.

lessons.title: 8.2 Linear Inequalities
lessons.html:
📖 Linear Inequalities
Solve exactly like an equation, with one rule that catches everyone.

Key Words & Meanings

Tap a word to open its definition.

Linear Inequalities

Comparisons producing a range of values rather than one equality.

variable

A symbol representing an unknown or changing quantity.

equation

A statement that two mathematical expressions have equal value.

verification

Checking a result in the original conditions to confirm it is valid.

Inequalities follow the same steps as equations, except that multiplying or dividing both sides by a negative number reverses the inequality sign.

Solutions are ranges rather than single values. On a number line, < and > take an open circle; ≤ and ≥ take a closed one.

Key points

  • Multiplying or dividing by a negative flips the sign.
  • Adding or subtracting never flips it.
  • Solutions are intervals, not single values.
  • Open circle for strict inequalities, closed for ≤ and ≥.
  • “At least” means ≥; “at most” means ≤; “more than” means >.
  • Check by substituting any value from your range.

Example

−2x + 3 > 11. Subtract 3: −2x > 8. Divide by −2 and flip: x < −4. Forgetting the flip gives x > −4, which is the trap answer offered every time.

Why this matters

Inequalities appear alone and inside word problems about budgets, capacities and minimum requirements, where the phrase-to-symbol translation matters as much as the algebra.

lessons.title: 8.3 Systems of Equations
lessons.html:
📖 Systems of Equations
Two equations, two unknowns — substitute or eliminate, whichever is tidier.

Key Words & Meanings

Tap a word to open its definition.

Systems of Equations

Two or more equations solved together for shared values.

variable

A symbol representing an unknown or changing quantity.

equation

A statement that two mathematical expressions have equal value.

verification

Checking a result in the original conditions to confirm it is valid.

A system asks for the values satisfying both equations at once, which graphically is where the two lines meet. Solve by substitution (isolate one variable and substitute) or elimination (add or subtract to cancel a variable).

Choose by shape: substitution when a variable is already isolated or has coefficient 1; elimination when coefficients line up or can be matched easily.

Key points

  • Substitution: isolate one variable, put it into the other equation.
  • Elimination: add or subtract the equations to cancel one variable.
  • The solution is the point where the lines intersect.
  • Parallel lines (same slope, different intercept) → no solution.
  • Identical lines → infinitely many solutions.
  • Desmos solves these instantly by graphing both equations.

Example

x + y = 10 and 2x − y = 5. Adding eliminates y: 3x = 15, so x = 5, and then y = 5. The pair (5, 5) satisfies both.

Why this matters

Systems are a guaranteed presence in the Algebra domain, and the no-solution / infinite-solution cases are tested as concept questions rather than computations.

lessons.title: 8.4 Functions
lessons.html:
📖 Functions
A function is a rule: one input, exactly one output.

Key Words & Meanings

Tap a word to open its definition.

Functions

Rules assigning exactly one output to each allowed input.

variable

A symbol representing an unknown or changing quantity.

equation

A statement that two mathematical expressions have equal value.

verification

Checking a result in the original conditions to confirm it is valid.

f(x) is notation, not multiplication. f(3) means substitute 3 wherever x appears. The domain is the allowed inputs; the range is the outputs produced.

Composite functions apply one rule then another: f(g(2)) means evaluate g at 2 first, then apply f to that result. Work from the inside out.

Key points

  • f(x) means the output of the rule f for input x — never f times x.
  • To evaluate, substitute the value everywhere x appears.
  • Composite: work inside out — f(g(2)) needs g(2) first.
  • Domain excludes anything making a denominator zero or a square root negative.
  • The vertical line test: a graph is a function if no vertical line meets it twice.
  • Finding x when f(x) = k means solving the equation, not evaluating it.

Example

If f(x) = 2x + 1 and g(x) = x², then f(g(3)) = f(9) = 2(9) + 1 = 19. Reversing the order gives g(f(3)) = g(7) = 49 — a different question with a different answer.

Why this matters

Function notation runs through Algebra and Advanced Math, and the inside-out rule for composites is tested every time it appears.

lessons.title: 8.5 Graphs
lessons.html:
📖 Graphs
Slope and intercept tell you almost everything a linear graph can say.

Key Words & Meanings

Tap a word to open its definition.

Graphs

Visual representations of relationships between variables.

variable

A symbol representing an unknown or changing quantity.

equation

A statement that two mathematical expressions have equal value.

verification

Checking a result in the original conditions to confirm it is valid.

In y = mx + b, m is the slope and b the y-intercept. Slope is rise over run: (y₂−y₁)/(x₂−x₁). This formula is not on the reference sheet.

In context questions, slope is a rate of change and the intercept is a starting value. Reading a word problem into those two roles solves most linear-modelling questions immediately.

Key points

  • y = mx + b: m is slope, b is where the line crosses the y-axis.
  • Slope = (y₂−y₁)/(x₂−x₁) — memorise it, it is not provided.
  • Positive slope rises left to right; negative falls; zero is horizontal.
  • A vertical line has undefined slope.
  • Parallel lines share a slope; perpendicular slopes multiply to −1.
  • In context: slope = rate of change, intercept = starting value.

Example

A phone plan costs $15 plus $0.10 per minute: y = 0.10x + 15. The intercept 15 is the fixed monthly charge and the slope 0.10 is the cost per minute — the two roles the SAT asks you to identify.

Why this matters

Linear graphs and their interpretation appear throughout Algebra and again in Problem Solving and Data Analysis as modelling questions.

lessons.title: 8.6 Quadratic Equations
lessons.html:
📖 Quadratic Equations
Three methods; pick the one the numbers invite.

Key Words & Meanings

Tap a word to open its definition.

Quadratic Equations

Second-degree equations containing a nonzero squared-variable term.

variable

A symbol representing an unknown or changing quantity.

equation

A statement that two mathematical expressions have equal value.

verification

Checking a result in the original conditions to confirm it is valid.

A quadratic has the form ax² + bx + c = 0. Solve by factoring when the numbers are friendly, by the quadratic formula when they are not, or by graphing in Desmos to read the x-intercepts.

The quadratic formula is x = (−b ± √(b²−4ac)) / 2a and is not on the reference sheet. The discriminant b²−4ac alone tells you how many real solutions exist.

Key points

  • Factor first if the numbers are small — it is fastest.
  • Quadratic formula always works: memorise it, it is not provided.
  • Discriminant > 0 → two real solutions; = 0 → one; < 0 → none.
  • The solutions are the x-intercepts of the parabola.
  • Set the equation to zero before doing anything else.
  • Desmos reads the roots straight off a graph.

Example

x² − 5x + 6 = 0 factors to (x−2)(x−3) = 0, giving x = 2 or x = 3. The discriminant is 25 − 24 = 1, positive, confirming two real solutions before any work.

Why this matters

Quadratics are the core of Advanced Math and appear in Algebra as well, in equations, functions and modelling questions alike.

lessons.title: 8.7 Polynomial Expressions
lessons.html:
📖 Polynomial Expressions
Combine like terms, distribute carefully, and watch the signs.

Key Words & Meanings

Tap a word to open its definition.

Polynomial Expressions

Sums of terms with variables raised to whole-number powers.

variable

A symbol representing an unknown or changing quantity.

equation

A statement that two mathematical expressions have equal value.

verification

Checking a result in the original conditions to confirm it is valid.

A polynomial is a sum of terms of the form axn. Adding and subtracting means combining like terms — those with the same variable and exponent. Multiplying means distributing every term across every other.

The commonest error is a sign: subtracting a polynomial requires distributing the minus sign across every term inside the brackets, not just the first.

Key points

  • Like terms share the same variable and exponent: 3x² and 5x², not 3x² and 3x.
  • Subtracting a polynomial distributes the minus across every term.
  • Multiply two binomials by distributing each term (FOIL).
  • The degree of a polynomial is its highest exponent.
  • Common factoring patterns: difference of squares, common factor, trinomials.
  • Check by substituting a simple value such as x = 1 or x = 2 into both forms.

Example

(3x² + 2x) − (x² − 4x) = 3x² + 2x − x² + 4x = 2x² + 6x. Failing to flip the sign on −4x gives 2x² − 2x, the standard wrong answer.

Why this matters

Polynomial manipulation supports factoring, quadratics and rational expressions, so an error habit here spreads across the whole Advanced Math domain.

lessons.title: 8.8 Word Problems
lessons.html:
📖 Word Problems
Translate the sentence into an equation before you calculate anything.

Key Words & Meanings

Tap a word to open its definition.

Word Problems

Real situations translated into mathematical relationships.

variable

A symbol representing an unknown or changing quantity.

equation

A statement that two mathematical expressions have equal value.

verification

Checking a result in the original conditions to confirm it is valid.

Most Math word problems fail at translation, not arithmetic. Read once for the situation, then identify what the unknown is, name it, and build an equation phrase by phrase.

The key phrases are consistent: is means equals, of means multiply, per means divide or a rate, more than means add, less than reverses the order of subtraction.

Key points

  • Name the unknown explicitly: let x = the number of hectares.
  • is → =, of → ×, per → rate, more than → +.
  • “5 less than x” is x − 5, not 5 − x.
  • Check what the question actually asks — often not the variable you solved for.
  • Include units and confirm the answer is plausible in context.
  • Rate problems: distance = rate × time; work = rate × time.

Example

“Seven less than three times a number is 14.” Let the number be x: 3x − 7 = 14, so 3x = 21 and x = 7. Writing 7 − 3x instead is the classic translation error.

Why this matters

Word problems are distributed across every Math domain. Translating carefully is worth more than any calculation shortcut, because a correctly built equation is nearly always easy to solve.

lessons.title: 9.1 Quadratic Functions
lessons.html:
📖 Quadratic Functions
The same equation in three forms, each telling you something different.

Key Words & Meanings

Tap a word to open its definition.

Quadratic Functions

Functions whose graphs are parabolas.

variable

A symbol representing an unknown or changing quantity.

equation

A statement that two mathematical expressions have equal value.

verification

Checking a result in the original conditions to confirm it is valid.

Standard form y = ax² + bx + c shows the y-intercept c. Factored form y = a(x−p)(x−q) shows the x-intercepts p and q. Vertex form y = a(x−h)² + k shows the vertex (h, k).

The SAT asks which form reveals a given feature most readily. The axis of symmetry is x = −b/2a, and the vertex lies on it. If a > 0 the parabola opens upward and the vertex is a minimum; if a < 0 it opens downward and the vertex is a maximum.

Key points

  • Standard form reveals the y-intercept.
  • Factored form reveals the x-intercepts.
  • Vertex form reveals the vertex, the maximum or minimum.
  • Axis of symmetry: x = −b/2a.
  • a > 0 opens upward (minimum); a < 0 opens downward (maximum).
  • The vertex x-value gives the input at which the output is largest or smallest.

Example

y = −2(x − 3)² + 8 is in vertex form: the vertex is (3, 8) and, because a is negative, that 8 is a maximum. No calculation needed — the form states it.

Why this matters

Quadratic functions are central to Advanced Math, and 'which form shows this feature' is a question type in its own right.

lessons.title: 9.2 Exponential Functions
lessons.html:
📖 Exponential Functions
Repeated multiplication, not repeated addition — that is the whole distinction.

Key Words & Meanings

Tap a word to open its definition.

Exponential Functions

Functions in which the variable appears in the exponent.

variable

A symbol representing an unknown or changing quantity.

equation

A statement that two mathematical expressions have equal value.

verification

Checking a result in the original conditions to confirm it is valid.

An exponential function has the form y = a·bx, where a is the starting value and b the growth factor. If b > 1 the quantity grows; if 0 < b < 1 it decays.

The SAT tests the contrast with linear models constantly. A linear model adds the same amount each period; an exponential model multiplies by the same factor each period.

Key points

  • y = a·bx: a is the initial value, b the factor per period.
  • b > 1 is growth; 0 < b < 1 is decay.
  • Growth of 5% per year → b = 1.05. Decay of 5% → b = 0.95.
  • Linear adds a constant; exponential multiplies by a constant.
  • At x = 0 the value is a, the y-intercept.
  • “Doubles each period” means b = 2; “halves” means b = 0.5.

Example

A population of 500 grows 8% per year: P = 500(1.08)t. After 3 years, 500(1.08)³ ≈ 630. A linear model adding 8% of the original each year would give 620 — close, and wrong.

Why this matters

Exponential models appear in Advanced Math and in the data-analysis questions about growth, decay and compound interest.

lessons.title: 9.3 Nonlinear Equations
lessons.html:
📖 Nonlinear Equations
When the graph is not a line, the number of solutions is part of the question.

Key Words & Meanings

Tap a word to open its definition.

Nonlinear Equations

Equations whose graphs are not straight lines.

variable

A symbol representing an unknown or changing quantity.

equation

A statement that two mathematical expressions have equal value.

verification

Checking a result in the original conditions to confirm it is valid.

Nonlinear equations include quadratics, higher-degree polynomials, radicals and rational equations. Their graphs curve, so a system pairing a line with a curve may have two solutions, one, or none.

Radical and rational equations require a check: squaring both sides or clearing a denominator can introduce extraneous solutions that satisfy the new equation but not the original.

Key points

  • A line and a parabola may intersect twice, once, or not at all.
  • Always substitute solutions back into the original equation.
  • Squaring both sides can create extraneous solutions.
  • Clearing a denominator can create a solution that makes it zero — reject it.
  • Desmos shows the number of intersections immediately.
  • Set one side to zero and find x-intercepts when solving graphically.

Example

√(x + 6) = x. Squaring gives x² − x − 6 = 0, so x = 3 or x = −2. Checking, √9 = 3 ✓ but √4 = 2 ≠ −2 ✗. Only x = 3 is a solution.

Why this matters

The extraneous-solution check is tested deliberately: the SAT offers the rejected value as an answer choice every time.

lessons.title: 9.4 Rational Expressions
lessons.html:
📖 Rational Expressions
A fraction with variables — and a denominator that must never be zero.

Key Words & Meanings

Tap a word to open its definition.

Rational Expressions

Fractions whose numerator or denominator contains polynomials.

variable

A symbol representing an unknown or changing quantity.

equation

A statement that two mathematical expressions have equal value.

verification

Checking a result in the original conditions to confirm it is valid.

Rational expressions are ratios of polynomials. Simplify by factoring the top and bottom and cancelling common factors. Only factors cancel, never individual terms.

Any value making the original denominator zero is excluded from the domain, and remains excluded even after cancelling.

Key points

  • Factor fully before cancelling anything.
  • Cancel factors, never terms across a plus or minus sign.
  • Excluded values come from the original denominator.
  • Add or subtract only over a common denominator.
  • Divide by multiplying by the reciprocal.
  • The expression is undefined wherever the denominator equals zero.

Example

(x² − 9)/(x − 3) = (x−3)(x+3)/(x−3) = x + 3, but x = 3 is still excluded because the original denominator was zero there.

Why this matters

Rational expressions appear in Advanced Math, and the excluded-value point is tested as a concept question far more often than the algebra itself.

lessons.title: 9.5 Radicals
lessons.html:
📖 M9:Radicals
Radical equations at Advanced Math level: isolate, square, and always check.

Key Words & Meanings

Tap a word to open its definition.

Radicals

Root expressions used in advanced equations and transformations.

variable

A symbol representing an unknown or changing quantity.

equation

A statement that two mathematical expressions have equal value.

verification

Checking a result in the original conditions to confirm it is valid.

Module 7 covered simplifying radicals. Here they appear inside equations, where the method is to isolate the radical first, then square both sides, then solve what remains.

Squaring is the dangerous step. It can turn a false statement into a true one, so every solution must be substituted back into the original equation. The SAT reliably offers the extraneous root as a choice.

Key points

  • Isolate the radical before squaring — never square a sum term by term.
  • (√a)² = a, but (a + √b)² requires full expansion.
  • Squaring may create extraneous solutions; check every answer.
  • Two radicals may need squaring twice, isolating one each time.
  • A square root cannot equal a negative number.
  • Fractional exponents are radicals: x2/3 = 3√(x²).

Example

√(2x + 3) − 1 = 4. Isolate: √(2x + 3) = 5. Square: 2x + 3 = 25. Solve: x = 11. Check: √25 − 1 = 4 ✓. Squaring before isolating would have produced a much messier and wrong equation.

Why this matters

Radical equations combine the exponent rules, the extraneous-root check and careful algebra, which is why they appear at the harder end of the Math section.

lessons.title: 9.6 Factoring
lessons.html:
📖 Factoring
Recognise the pattern and the factorisation writes itself.

Key Words & Meanings

Tap a word to open its definition.

Factoring

Rewriting an expression as a product of simpler factors.

variable

A symbol representing an unknown or changing quantity.

equation

A statement that two mathematical expressions have equal value.

verification

Checking a result in the original conditions to confirm it is valid.

Factoring reverses multiplication. Always look for a common factor first, then check for a recognisable pattern before attempting trial and error.

The three patterns worth knowing cold are the difference of squares, the perfect-square trinomial, and the simple trinomial where you seek two numbers multiplying to c and adding to b.

Key points

  • Common factor first: 2x² + 6x = 2x(x + 3).
  • Difference of squares: a² − b² = (a−b)(a+b).
  • Perfect square: a² ± 2ab + b² = (a ± b)².
  • Simple trinomial x² + bx + c: find two numbers multiplying to c, adding to b.
  • A sum of squares a² + b² does not factor over the reals.
  • Check by expanding your factors back out.

Example

x² − 16 is a difference of squares: (x − 4)(x + 4). But x² + 16 does not factor at all over the real numbers — a distinction the SAT tests directly.

Why this matters

Factoring underlies quadratics, rational expressions and polynomial questions, so pattern recognition here speeds up the whole Advanced Math domain.

lessons.title: 9.7 Advanced Word Problems
lessons.html:
📖 Advanced Word Problems
Harder wrapping, same method: name the unknown and build the equation.

Key Words & Meanings

Tap a word to open its definition.

Advanced Word Problems

Multi-step situations requiring algebraic modeling and interpretation.

variable

A symbol representing an unknown or changing quantity.

equation

A statement that two mathematical expressions have equal value.

verification

Checking a result in the original conditions to confirm it is valid.

Advanced word problems involve quadratic, exponential or systems models rather than single linear equations. The translation discipline is identical; only the model changes.

Read for the shape of the relationship. Constant addition per period means linear. Constant multiplication means exponential. A product of two varying quantities, or an area, usually means quadratic.

Key points

  • Constant amount per period → linear model.
  • Constant percentage or factor per period → exponential model.
  • Area, product of two changing quantities, or projectile height → quadratic.
  • Two unknowns with two conditions → a system.
  • Define every variable in words before writing any equation.
  • Reject solutions that are impossible in context, such as a negative length.

Example

A rectangular plot has a perimeter of 40 m and an area of 96 m². Let width be w: length is 20 − w, so w(20 − w) = 96, giving w² − 20w + 96 = 0 and w = 8 or 12. Both are valid — the same rectangle, 8 m by 12 m.

Why this matters

These questions sit at the top of the Math difficulty range, and the marks go to candidates who identify the model before touching the algebra.

lessons.title: 10.1 Ratios
lessons.html:
📖 M10:Ratios
Ratios in context: rates, unit conversions and scaling.

Key Words & Meanings

Tap a word to open its definition.

Ratios

Comparisons showing the relative size of two quantities.

dataset

A collection of values gathered for analysis.

variable

A characteristic or quantity that can change.

interpretation

A conclusion drawn carefully from mathematical evidence.

Module 7 covered the mechanics; here ratios appear as rates — kilometres per hour, dollars per kilogram, people per square kilometre — and as scale factors in maps and models.

The reliable technique is to set up the ratio with units written in, then cancel units the way you cancel numbers. If the units of your answer are wrong, the setup is wrong regardless of the arithmetic.

Key points

  • Write units into every ratio and cancel them as you would numbers.
  • A unit rate has 1 in the denominator: cost per item, distance per hour.
  • To convert, multiply by a fraction equal to 1: 1 km / 1000 m.
  • Scale factor for length k means area scales by k² and volume by k³.
  • Check plausibility: an answer thousands of times too large signals an inverted ratio.
  • Rates can be combined by adding work per unit time, not by adding times.

Example

A vehicle uses 6 litres per 100 km. For 250 km: 250 km × (6 L / 100 km) = 15 L. The km cancel, leaving litres — confirming the ratio was set up the right way up.

Why this matters

Rates and unit conversion appear throughout Problem Solving and Data Analysis, which is roughly a quarter of the Math section.

lessons.title: 10.2 Proportions
lessons.html:
📖 Proportions
Two equal ratios; cross-multiply and solve.

Key Words & Meanings

Tap a word to open its definition.

Proportions

Equations stating that two ratios are equal.

dataset

A collection of values gathered for analysis.

variable

A characteristic or quantity that can change.

interpretation

A conclusion drawn carefully from mathematical evidence.

A proportion states that two ratios are equal: a/b = c/d. Cross-multiplying gives ad = bc, which turns it into a linear equation.

Distinguish direct proportion, where one quantity rises as the other does (y = kx), from inverse proportion, where one falls as the other rises (y = k/x). More workers finishing a job faster is inverse, not direct.

Key points

  • Cross-multiply: a/b = c/d becomes ad = bc.
  • Keep corresponding quantities in matching positions.
  • Direct: y = kx, so y/x stays constant.
  • Inverse: y = k/x, so the product xy stays constant.
  • Similar figures give proportional corresponding sides.
  • Check the direction: does the answer being larger make sense?

Example

If 4 workers build a wall in 9 days, how long do 6 take? This is inverse: 4 × 9 = 36 worker-days, so 36 ÷ 6 = 6 days. Treating it as direct would give 13.5 — more workers taking longer.

Why this matters

Proportional reasoning appears in geometry through similar triangles and throughout data analysis in scaling and rate questions.

lessons.title: 10.3 Percent Problems
lessons.html:
📖 Percent Problems
Percent in context: discounts, interest, markups and change over time.

Key Words & Meanings

Tap a word to open its definition.

Percent Problems

Problems involving parts per hundred, increases, decreases, or repeated change.

dataset

A collection of values gathered for analysis.

variable

A characteristic or quantity that can change.

interpretation

A conclusion drawn carefully from mathematical evidence.

Module 7 covered the arithmetic; here percentages appear inside situations. The three commonest are a discount then tax, simple versus compound interest, and percent change between two reported figures.

Compound interest is exponential: A = P(1 + r)t. Simple interest is linear: A = P(1 + rt). The SAT tests the difference deliberately.

Key points

  • Discount of d% then tax of t%: multiply by (1−d) then (1+t).
  • Successive percentages multiply; they never add.
  • Compound: A = P(1 + r)t. Simple: A = P(1 + rt).
  • Percent change = (new − old) ÷ old × 100.
  • To find the original before an increase, divide by (1 + rate).
  • Percentage points and percent are different: 20% to 25% is 5 points but a 25% increase.

Example

An item priced $200 is discounted 15% then taxed 8%: 200 × 0.85 × 1.08 = $183.60. Combining into a single 7% reduction gives $186 — close enough to be tempting and wrong.

Why this matters

Percent-in-context problems are among the most frequent in Problem Solving and Data Analysis, and the multiply-don't-add rule settles most of them.

questions.explanation: Apply the factors in turn: 200 × 0.85 × 1.08 = $183.60.

questions.explanation: Compound interest multiplies by (1 + r) each period, which is exponential growth.

options: An increase of 5 percentage points, or 25%
questions.explanation: The absolute change is 5 percentage points, which is a 25% relative increase on the original 20%.

lessons.title: 10.4 Statistics
lessons.html:
📖 Statistics
Mean, median, mode and spread — and knowing which one an outlier moves.

Key Words & Meanings

Tap a word to open its definition.

Statistics

Methods for describing, organizing, and interpreting data.

dataset

A collection of values gathered for analysis.

variable

A characteristic or quantity that can change.

interpretation

A conclusion drawn carefully from mathematical evidence.

The mean is the average, the median the middle value when ordered, the mode the most frequent. The range is largest minus smallest, and standard deviation measures how spread out values are.

The SAT's favourite point here is that the mean is pulled by extreme values while the median is not. Questions about skewed data almost always turn on that.

Key points

  • Mean = sum ÷ count. Median = middle of the ordered list.
  • With an even count, the median is the average of the two middle values.
  • An outlier moves the mean, not the median.
  • Standard deviation measures spread; a tighter cluster means a smaller value.
  • Adding the same constant to every value shifts the mean but not the spread.
  • You are never asked to compute standard deviation, only to compare it.

Example

Incomes 20, 22, 24, 26, 400 (thousands): the median is 24 and the mean is 98.4. One extreme value has made the mean describe nobody in the list. That is why median is reported for incomes.

Why this matters

Statistics questions in Problem Solving and Data Analysis are usually conceptual rather than computational, so understanding beats arithmetic here.

options: The mean best represents the data

options: Changes the standard deviation but not the mean
Changes the mean but not the standard deviation

questions.explanation: The mean uses every value in its sum, so a single extreme value shifts it substantially.

lessons.title: 10.5 Probability
lessons.html:
📖 Probability
Favourable outcomes over total outcomes — and read the table carefully.

Key Words & Meanings

Tap a word to open its definition.

Probability

A numerical measure of how likely an event is.

dataset

A collection of values gathered for analysis.

variable

A characteristic or quantity that can change.

interpretation

A conclusion drawn carefully from mathematical evidence.

Probability is the number of favourable outcomes divided by the total number of equally likely outcomes, always between 0 and 1. The probability that an event does not happen is 1 minus the probability that it does.

Most SAT probability questions are two-way table questions. The difficulty is not the arithmetic but identifying the correct denominator: the whole table, one row, or one column.

Key points

  • P(event) = favourable ÷ total, always between 0 and 1.
  • P(not A) = 1 − P(A).
  • For independent events, multiply: P(A and B) = P(A) × P(B).
  • In two-way tables, the wording fixes the denominator.
  • “Of those who…” restricts you to that row or column.
  • Express the answer as the question asks: fraction, decimal or percent.

Example

A table shows 40 students, 25 of them female, 10 of those female students studying science. P(science given female) = 10/25 = 0.4, not 10/40. The words “of the female students” changed the denominator.

Why this matters

Two-way table probability appears in nearly every Math section, and the denominator error is the single most common mistake made on it.

questions.explanation: The condition 'given female' restricts the denominator to the 25 female students.

questions.explanation: The complement of an event has probability 1 − P(A) = 0.7.

questions.question: For two independent events, P(A and B) equals:
questions.explanation: Independent events combine multiplicatively for the probability that both occur.

lessons.title: 10.6 Data Interpretation
lessons.html:
📖 Data Interpretation
Read what the graphic shows, not what you expect it to show.

Key Words & Meanings

Tap a word to open its definition.

Data Interpretation

The process of extracting accurate meaning from presented data.

dataset

A collection of values gathered for analysis.

variable

A characteristic or quantity that can change.

interpretation

A conclusion drawn carefully from mathematical evidence.

Data questions give you a table, graph or chart and ask what it supports. No advanced mathematics is needed; the marks are lost to careless reading of labels, units and scales.

A broken or non-zero axis exaggerates differences visually. A logarithmic scale compresses them. Always check where the axis starts before judging how big a change looks.

Key points

  • Read title, axis labels, units and legend before the choices.
  • Check where the vertical axis starts — a truncated axis exaggerates change.
  • Counts, percentages and rates are different things.
  • Only conclude what the data shows; correlation is not causation.
  • A trend over the shown period says nothing about outside it.
  • For “consistent with the data”, verify the numbers rather than the wording.

Example

A bar chart with a vertical axis starting at 95 makes 96 look twice 95. The visual difference is a scale artefact; the actual difference is about 1%. The SAT offers a choice describing it as a “dramatic increase”.

Why this matters

Data interpretation appears in both Math and Reading & Writing, and rewards nothing but disciplined reading of the labels.

options: A scale artefact; the real difference is about 1%

options: The axis labels, units and starting value
questions.explanation: Units and axis range determine whether an apparent difference is real or a display effect.

lessons.title: 10.7 Tables and Charts
lessons.html:
📖 Tables and Charts
Two-way tables reward finding the right row, column and total.

Key Words & Meanings

Tap a word to open its definition.

Tables and Charts

Structured visual displays used to organize and compare values.

dataset

A collection of values gathered for analysis.

variable

A characteristic or quantity that can change.

interpretation

A conclusion drawn carefully from mathematical evidence.

A two-way table cross-classifies data by two variables. Every question about one is answered by identifying three numbers: the count you want, the relevant total, and the relationship between them.

Row totals, column totals and the grand total are all present. The wording of the question tells you which is the denominator, and getting that wrong is the standard error.

Key points

  • Identify the row, the column and the total the question needs.
  • “Of all participants” → grand total. “Of the men” → that row's total.
  • Check that row and column totals add to the grand total before relying on them.
  • Bar charts compare categories; line graphs show change over time; pie charts show shares of a whole.
  • A pie chart's slices must sum to 100%.
  • Convert to the form the question asks for: fraction, decimal or percentage.

Example

A table shows 120 respondents, 70 rural, and 42 of the rural group owning a phone. “What percentage of rural respondents own a phone?” is 42/70 = 60%. Using 120 gives 35%, which answers a different question.

Why this matters

Table questions are among the most numerous in Problem Solving and Data Analysis, and every one turns on choosing the correct denominator.

questions.explanation: The question restricts to rural respondents, so the denominator is 70: 42/70 = 60%.

questions.explanation: The condition restricts the population to that group, making its total the denominator.

lessons.title: 10.8 Scatterplots
lessons.html:
📖 Scatterplots
Points show a relationship; the line of best fit summarises it.

Key Words & Meanings

Tap a word to open its definition.

Scatterplots

Graphs showing the relationship between two quantitative variables.

dataset

A collection of values gathered for analysis.

variable

A characteristic or quantity that can change.

interpretation

A conclusion drawn carefully from mathematical evidence.

A scatterplot plots one variable against another to reveal association. The line of best fit models the overall trend, and its slope is the predicted change in y for each unit increase in x.

Association is not causation. A strong pattern shows the two variables move together; it says nothing about which, if either, causes the other.

Key points

  • Positive association rises left to right; negative falls; no association shows no pattern.
  • The line of best fit models the trend, not any individual point.
  • Its slope = predicted change in y per one-unit increase in x.
  • Its y-intercept = predicted y when x is zero, which may be meaningless in context.
  • A residual is actual minus predicted; a point above the line has a positive residual.
  • Correlation never establishes causation.

Example

A scatterplot of fertiliser against yield has a best-fit line of slope 0.8. Each additional unit of fertiliser predicts 0.8 more tonnes. A field yielding 3 tonnes above the line has a positive residual of 3.

Why this matters

Scatterplots and lines of best fit recur throughout Problem Solving and Data Analysis, and the slope-as-rate interpretation is tested every time.

questions.explanation: The slope of a best-fit line is the predicted change in y for each one-unit increase in x.

questions.explanation: The residual is actual minus predicted, which is positive for a point above the line.

questions.question: A strong positive correlation between two variables shows that:
questions.explanation: Correlation describes association only; it does not establish that one variable causes the other.

lessons.title: 10.9 Real-Life Applications
lessons.html:
📖 Real-Life Applications
Context questions test whether you can read a situation into a model.

Key Words & Meanings

Tap a word to open its definition.

Real-Life Applications

Mathematical models used to solve practical situations.

dataset

A collection of values gathered for analysis.

variable

A characteristic or quantity that can change.

interpretation

A conclusion drawn carefully from mathematical evidence.

These questions wrap the mathematics in a scenario: budgets, fuel, wages, population, dosage. The work is identifying which model applies and what each number in it means.

Interpretation questions are common: given a model, what does a particular coefficient represent? The answer is always a rate, a starting value, or a total, and the units tell you which.

Key points

  • Fixed amount plus a rate → linear: y = mx + b.
  • Constant percentage change → exponential: y = a·bx.
  • The constant term is usually a starting or fixed value.
  • The coefficient on the variable is usually a rate — check its units.
  • Confirm your answer is plausible in the real situation.
  • Answer the question asked, which is often not the variable you solved for.

Example

A generator model is C = 45t + 300, cost in dollars for t hours. The 300 is the fixed hire charge and the 45 is dollars per hour of running. Reading the units off the equation answers the interpretation question directly.

Why this matters

Modelling and interpretation questions are heavily represented on the Digital SAT, and they reward reading comprehension applied to algebra rather than harder algebra.

lessons.title: 11.1 Lines and Angles
lessons.html:
📖 Lines and Angles
A handful of angle relationships settles most geometry setups.

Key Words & Meanings

Tap a word to open its definition.

Lines and Angles

Geometric relationships involving straight paths, intersections, and rotations.

dimension

A measurable length, width, height, or radius.

theorem

A mathematical statement proved to be true.

diagram

A labeled drawing representing geometric information.

Angles on a straight line sum to 180°; angles round a point sum to 360°. Vertical angles — opposite each other where two lines cross — are equal.

When a transversal cuts parallel lines, corresponding and alternate angles are equal, and co-interior angles sum to 180°. Most SAT geometry diagrams are built from exactly these facts.

Key points

  • Angles on a straight line sum to 180°.
  • Angles around a point sum to 360°.
  • Vertical (opposite) angles are equal.
  • With parallel lines: corresponding and alternate angles are equal.
  • Co-interior (same-side) angles sum to 180°.
  • Complementary angles sum to 90°; supplementary to 180°.

Example

A transversal crosses two parallel lines and one angle is 70°. Its vertical angle is 70°, its corresponding angle is 70°, and each co-interior angle is 110° — the whole diagram from one measurement.

Why this matters

Angle relationships are the entry point to nearly every geometry question, including triangle and circle problems that look harder than they are.

questions.explanation: Co-interior angles on the same side of a transversal between parallel lines sum to 180°.

questions.explanation: Opposite angles at an intersection are always equal.

questions.question: Angles around a point sum to:
questions.explanation: A full turn about a point measures 360°.

lessons.title: 11.2 Triangles
lessons.html:
📖 Triangles
Angle sum, Pythagoras and similarity cover almost every triangle question.

Key Words & Meanings

Tap a word to open its definition.

Triangles

Three-sided polygons governed by angle, side, and area relationships.

dimension

A measurable length, width, height, or radius.

theorem

A mathematical statement proved to be true.

diagram

A labeled drawing representing geometric information.

A triangle's angles sum to 180°. An exterior angle equals the sum of the two opposite interior angles. In a right triangle, a² + b² = c², with c the hypotenuse.

Similar triangles have equal angles and proportional sides — the basis of most multi-step geometry questions. The Pythagorean theorem and special right triangles are on the Bluebook reference sheet.

Key points

  • Interior angles sum to 180°.
  • An exterior angle equals the sum of the two remote interior angles.
  • Pythagoras: a² + b² = c², c opposite the right angle.
  • Common triples: 3-4-5, 5-12-13, 8-15-17 and their multiples.
  • Special triangles: 30-60-90 sides are x, x√3, 2x; 45-45-90 are x, x, x√2.
  • Similar triangles have proportional corresponding sides.

Example

A right triangle has legs 6 and 8. Rather than computing, recognise 6-8-10 as a doubled 3-4-5 triple: the hypotenuse is 10. Recognising triples saves time on a section where time is the constraint.

Why this matters

Triangles appear in coordinate geometry, trigonometry and area questions, so the same few facts get reused throughout the geometry domain.

lessons.html: Quick check: Review the lesson notes and work the two practice questions, then answer these to confirm you understood Triangles.

questions.explanation: 6-8-10 is a multiple of the 3-4-5 triple, so the hypotenuse is 10.

questions.explanation: The sides opposite 30°, 60° and 90° are in the ratio 1 : √3 : 2.

options: The sum of the two remote interior angles
questions.explanation: The exterior angle theorem states it equals the sum of the two non-adjacent interior angles.

lessons.title: 11.3 Circles
lessons.html:
📖 Circles
Radius drives everything; the reference sheet supplies the formulas.

Key Words & Meanings

Tap a word to open its definition.

Circles

Sets of points equally distant from a center.

dimension

A measurable length, width, height, or radius.

theorem

A mathematical statement proved to be true.

diagram

A labeled drawing representing geometric information.

Area is πr² and circumference is 2πr, both on the Bluebook reference sheet. Arc length and sector area are fractions of those, set by the central angle over 360°.

In coordinate geometry, a circle centred at (h, k) with radius r has equation (x−h)² + (y−k)² = r². This equation is not on the reference sheet.

Key points

  • Area = πr²; circumference = 2πr; diameter = 2r.
  • Arc length = (angle/360) × circumference.
  • Sector area = (angle/360) × area.
  • Circle equation: (x−h)² + (y−k)² = r² — memorise it.
  • A radius drawn to the point of tangency is perpendicular to the tangent.
  • An inscribed angle is half the central angle on the same arc.

Example

A circle of radius 6 with a 60° sector: the sector is 60/360 = 1/6 of the circle, so its area is (1/6)π(36) = 6π.

Why this matters

Circle questions appear in both plane and coordinate geometry, and the circle equation is one of the few geometry formulas you must actually memorise.

questions.explanation: The sector is 60/360 = 1/6 of the circle, so its area is (1/6)(36π) = 6π.

questions.explanation: The form is (x − h)² + (y − k)² = r², with h = 2, k = −3 and r² = 25.

questions.explanation: The radius meets a tangent line at right angles at the point of contact.

lessons.title: 11.4 Polygons
lessons.html:
📖 Polygons
Angle sums follow one formula; area usually means splitting the shape up.

Key Words & Meanings

Tap a word to open its definition.

Polygons

Closed plane figures made from straight line segments.

dimension

A measurable length, width, height, or radius.

theorem

A mathematical statement proved to be true.

diagram

A labeled drawing representing geometric information.

The interior angles of an n-sided polygon sum to (n − 2) × 180°. In a regular polygon all angles are equal, so each is that sum divided by n. Exterior angles always sum to 360°, whatever n is.

For area, the reference sheet gives rectangles, triangles and circles. Anything else you split into those shapes.

Key points

  • Interior angle sum = (n − 2) × 180°.
  • Each interior angle of a regular n-gon = (n − 2) × 180° ÷ n.
  • Exterior angles of any polygon sum to 360°.
  • Split irregular shapes into rectangles and triangles to find area.
  • A parallelogram's area is base × height, using perpendicular height.
  • A trapezoid's area is the average of the parallel sides times the height.

Example

A regular hexagon: n = 6, so the interior sum is (6−2) × 180 = 720°, and each angle is 720 ÷ 6 = 120°.

Why this matters

Polygon questions are formula-driven and quick once the angle-sum relation is memorised, which makes them dependable points in the geometry domain.

lessons.title: 📝 Practice: Polygons
lessons.html: Quick check: Review the lesson notes and work the two practice questions, then answer these to confirm you understood Polygons.

questions.explanation: The interior sum is (6 − 2) × 180 = 720°, and dividing by 6 gives 120°.

questions.question: The exterior angles of any polygon sum to:
questions.explanation: Regardless of the number of sides, exterior angles always total 360°.

questions.question: How do you find the area of an irregular shape on the SAT?
options: Split it into rectangles and triangles
questions.explanation: Decomposing into shapes whose formulas you have is the standard method.

lessons.title: 11.5 Coordinate Geometry
lessons.html:
📖 Coordinate Geometry
Algebra applied to the plane: distance, midpoint, slope and equations.

Key Words & Meanings

Tap a word to open its definition.

Coordinate Geometry

Study of geometric figures using points, equations, and a coordinate plane.

dimension

A measurable length, width, height, or radius.

theorem

A mathematical statement proved to be true.

diagram

A labeled drawing representing geometric information.

The distance between two points comes from Pythagoras: √((x₂−x₁)² + (y₂−y₁)²). The midpoint is the average of the coordinates.

Slope, parallel and perpendicular relationships, and the circle equation all appear here. None of these formulas is on the reference sheet, so they have to be learned.

Key points

  • Distance = √((x₂−x₁)² + (y₂−y₁)²).
  • Midpoint = ((x₁+x₂)/2, (y₁+y₂)/2).
  • Parallel lines share a slope; perpendicular slopes multiply to −1.
  • Circle: (x−h)² + (y−k)² = r².
  • The x-intercept has y = 0; the y-intercept has x = 0.
  • Desmos plots any of these instantly for checking.

Example

Distance from (1, 2) to (4, 6): differences 3 and 4, so √(9 + 16) = 5. Recognising the 3-4-5 triple gets you there without touching the calculator.

Why this matters

Coordinate geometry links the Algebra and Geometry domains, and its formulas are among the few the app does not supply.

questions.explanation: The differences are 3 and 4, giving √(9 + 16) = 5, a 3-4-5 triple.

questions.explanation: The midpoint averages each coordinate: ((2+8)/2, (4+10)/2) = (5, 7).

questions.explanation: Perpendicular slopes are negative reciprocals, so the slope is −1/2.

lessons.title: 11.6 Area and Volume
lessons.html:
📖 Area and Volume
The formulas are provided; knowing which one applies is the skill.

Key Words & Meanings

Tap a word to open its definition.

Area and Volume

Measures of two-dimensional surface and three-dimensional space.

dimension

A measurable length, width, height, or radius.

theorem

A mathematical statement proved to be true.

diagram

A labeled drawing representing geometric information.

The Bluebook reference sheet supplies areas of rectangles, triangles and circles, and volumes of rectangular solids, cylinders, spheres, cones and pyramids. You do not need to memorise them.

What you do need is to identify the solid, extract the right measurements, and watch the scaling rule: multiplying every length by k multiplies area by k² and volume by k³.

Key points

  • Reference sheet supplies area and volume formulas — use it.
  • Read whether a question gives radius or diameter; halve if needed.
  • Length scale factor k → area × k², volume × k³.
  • Surface area is the sum of the faces; volume is the space inside.
  • Composite solids: split them, compute each part, then add.
  • Keep units consistent before calculating, and state units in the answer.

Example

Double every dimension of a cube and the volume becomes 8 times larger, not twice. A 2×2×2 cube has volume 8; a 4×4×4 cube has volume 64.

Why this matters

Area and volume questions are usually about setup rather than formula recall, and the k²/k³ scaling rule is tested as a concept question every time it appears.
